passages.title: A Book to bring people into light
passages.tafsir:
**Sūrah Ibrāhīm opens by stating the Qur'an's purpose in one sentence: it was sent down so that the Prophet ﷺ could take humanity out of darkness into light.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that this fourteenth sūrah is Makkī, revealed before the Hijrah apart from some verses over which scholars differ. It opens with the mission of the messengers and prophets, and moves into tawḥīd (Allah's Oneness) and its proofs — and it is in that connection that the story of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) enters, which is why the sūrah carries his name.

## Alif, Lām, Rā

These are among the *al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt*, the "isolated letters" that open certain sūrahs. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets out the practice of the most righteous elders as the safest and most doubt-free course: believe firmly that whatever they mean or signify is true, but stay away from launching deeper investigations into their meanings.

## "A Book We have sent down to you"

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reads *Kitābun anzalnāhu ilayk* as the predicate of an understood *hādhā* — "**this** is a Book which We have sent down to you." The revelation of the Book is attributed to Allah Himself (*anzalnāhu*, "**We** sent it down"), which tells you the greatness of the Book; and it is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ (*ilayk*, "to **you**"), suggestive of his personal high station as its first addressee. Ibn Kathīr fills in the picture: the Glorious Qur'an, the most honoured Book, sent down from heaven to the most honoured Messenger, sent to all the people of the earth, Arabs and non-Arabs alike.

## Darkness in the plural, light in the singular

*An-nās* — "the people" — is used for humankind: all human beings present now or who will come in the future.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out the wording. *Aẓ-ẓulumāt* ("darknesses") is **plural**; *an-nūr* ("the light") is **singular**. The darknesses are those of *kufr* (infidelity, disbelief), of *shirk* (the ascribing of partners to Allah), and of evil deeds — plural, because there are many kinds and shades of kufr and shirk, and evil deeds too are countless. The light is the light of faith, singular because faith and truth are one and the same.

This is not physical darkness and light that could be seen with the naked eye. Ibn Kathīr renders the sense plainly: "We sent you, O Muhammad, with this Book in order that you might lead mankind away from misguidance and crookedness to guidance and the right way." He cites 2:257, where Allah is the *Walī* (Protector or Guardian) of the believers and brings them out from darkness into light, while the disbelievers' *awliyāʾ* are the *ṭāghūt* (false deities), who "bring them out from light into darkness" — the same movement in reverse. He cites 57:9 in the same connection.

## "By the leave of their Lord"

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān raises an obvious question. The verse makes taking people out of darkness the act of the Prophet ﷺ — yet giving guidance is in reality an act of Allah alone: "You cannot, on your own, give guidance to anyone, but it is Allah alone who gives guidance to whom He wills" (28:56). The phrase *bi-idhni Rabbihim*, "with the will of their Lord," eliminates the doubt: this act is not originally in your hands, but it shall be with the will and permission of Allah that you could do so. Ibn Kathīr says the same from the other side — Allah guides those whom He destined to be guided "by the hand of His Messenger ﷺ, whom He sent to guide them by His command."

Notice which name Allah chooses: not "by His leave," but "by the leave of **their Lord**." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reads this as pure mercy — there is no other reason behind this universal blessing except that He would let the human beings of the world be delivered from every such darkness through His Book and Messenger. Otherwise, Allah owes nothing to anyone, and there is no one who can force Him to do anything.

Guidance is Allah's act — yet by attributing it to the Prophet ﷺ, the verse also establishes that guidance cannot be received or acquired without his mediation. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's conclusion is blunt: only that sense or interpretation of the Qur'an is trustworthy which has been communicated to us by the Prophet ﷺ through his word or deed; any interpretation contrary to it is not reliable.

**One further note.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān holds that reciting the Qur'an's words, even without understanding them, registers a positive effect on the human self and helps the reciter stay safe against evils. Where the Qur'an describes the Prophet's ﷺ basic functions (3:164; 62:2), *tilāwah* (recitation) is mentioned separately and **ahead of** teaching the meanings — recitation being related to words, while meanings are understood rather than recited.

## "To the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy"

Ibn Kathīr: *al-ʿAzīz* is the One who can never be resisted or overpowered — rather, Allah is Irresistible above everything and everyone else. *Al-Ḥamīd* is the One who is glorified and praised in all His actions, statements, legislation, commandments and prohibitions, and who only says the truth in the information He conveys.

Why place these two ahead of the Name? Maʿārif ul Qurʾān answers that it is a hint about the road: the Pure and Sacred Being to whom this way is going to lead is Mighty and Overpowering, and deserving of all praise as well — therefore one who takes to this way will never falter or stumble anywhere en route, nor will the effort made on it ever go to waste. "The way of Allah" means exactly that — the way walking on which human beings could reach their Creator and achieve the ultimate degree of success, which is His pleasure.

## Whose path it is — and what "woe" means

*Allāhi'lladhī lahu mā fī's-samāwāti wa mā fī'l-arḍ* — Allah, the One to whom belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth; the Creator of everything in them, the absolute Sovereign having no partners or associates. Ibn Kathīr notes that this is similar to 7:158, "Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah — to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth."

Then the turn: *wa waylun li'l-kāfirīna min ʿadhābin shadīd*. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains *wayl* as used in the sense of severe punishment and fatal consequence; Ibn Kathīr, as woe on the Day of Judgement, "because they defied you, O Muhammad, and rejected you."

The warning obviously targets those who deny that the Qur'an is the Divine Word — but, adds Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, those who believe in it and yet have abandoned it in their practical life, never reciting it, never trying to understand it, never acting upon its teachings, "cannot be considered totally free and safe from becoming targets of this warning."

## The anatomy of refusal

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān identifies three states in which the deniers of the Qur'an are found.

**First: they prefer the life of this world to the Hereafter.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reads this as a hint towards the diagnosis of their disease, their chronic denial of the truth. Despite the all too manifest miracles of the Qur'an they remain hostile because their lust for life in the present world has blinded them; they are unable to visualise what would matter most in the Hereafter, and so they would tolerate any loss there for the sake of worldly gain. They covet the former life and work hard for its sake, says Ibn Kathīr, having forgotten the Hereafter and abandoned it behind their backs. They are quite content with the darkness they are in, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds, and towards light they do not care to come.

**Second: they hinder others from the path of Allah** — from following the Messengers, as Ibn Kathīr glosses it. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān calls this injustice upon injustice: having chosen those many layers of darkness for themselves, they then, to conceal their error, prevent others too from taking to the broad way of light.

**Third: they "seek crookedness in it."** Ibn Kathīr's meaning: they seek to make Allah's path crooked — looking for some fault in an otherwise radiant and straight path, whereby they might raise an objection or throw a taunt. Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī's reading, relayed by Maʿārif ul Qurʾān: they are always trying to find something in the way of Allah — that is, in the Qur'an and Sunnah — which could be in line with their own ideas and wishes.

That second reading applies to our own time. A fairly large number of educated people these days come up with the framework of an idea, then go about looking for its supporting evidence in the Qur'an and Sunnah. The method is wrong in principle. The believer's duty runs in the reverse order: **first unburden the mind of personal ideas and wishes, then consult the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ — and whatever stands proved clearly there becomes his personal creed.**

The passage ends *ulāʾika fī ḍalālin baʿīd*, "they are far away in straying": they have strayed out so far that it is now difficult for them to return to the right path. Ibn Kathīr adds that when the disbelievers do this they become engulfed in ignorance and misguidance far away from the truth, and therefore there is no hope that they will gain guidance while in that state.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī that although these three traits have been identified here with disbelievers, in terms of the principle involved any Muslim in whom they are present is likewise deserving of this warning. May Allah protect us from it.

## The mercy of a familiar tongue

"And We sent not a Messenger except with the language of his people, in order that he might make the Message clear for them."

Ibn Kathīr reads this as Allah being Kind and Compassionate with His creation: He sends Messengers to people **from among them**, speaking their language, so that they are able to understand the Message. Otherwise, notes Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, a people would have to undergo the burden of translating the injunctions before they could understand them. So the messenger sent to speakers of Hebrew spoke Hebrew; the messenger sent to the Persians, Persian; the messenger to the Berbers, Berberi. Sometimes it was the messenger's mother tongue; sometimes Allah arranged that he learn it, as with Lūṭ (peace be upon him), a citizen of ʿIrāq where the language spoken was Persian, who after his migration to Syria married among the people there so that the language of the Syrians became his own.

The mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stands apart. In terms of area it is for the whole world, and in terms of time it applies right up to the last day of Qiyāmah; no nation or group of people, whatever their country or language, falls outside the circle of his mission. Both Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cite the narration of Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him) recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs — the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and Muslim — in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "I have been given five things which were not given to Anyone else before me. Allah made me victorious by awe, (by His frightening my enemies) for a distance of one month's journey. The earth has been made for me (and for my followers) a place for worship and a purifier. The war booty has been made lawful for me and it was not lawful for anyone else before me. I have been given the right of Intercession (on the Day of Resurrection). Every Prophet used to be sent to his nation only, but I have been sent to all mankind."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets this in a longer arc. As human society grew, arrangements to convey right guidance through messengers and prophets kept being made, with injunctions, laws and religious codes suited to every period and every people. When the human scene reached maturity, Allah sent Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ as the Messenger to the whole world, and gave him a Book and a Sharīʿah in their most complete form, valid for all the world and all times: "Today, I have perfected your religion and made My favour complete for you" (5:3). The codes of the past prophets were perfect for their own time and region; but the perfection of this Sharīʿah is not restricted to a time or a region — and this is why the chain of prophethood was discontinued after the Prophet ﷺ, the Last of the blessed prophets.

## Then why Arabic?

If each people receives the message in its own tongue, why was the final, universal message given in Arabic? Revealing the Qur'an separately into the language of every group of people was not difficult at all for the most perfect power of Allah — but the great objective of one Rasūl, one Kitāb and one Sharīʿah, which sought to forge religious, moral and social unity among peoples divided by thousands of differences, would then have remained unrealised. And letting the Qur'an and Ḥadīth be available to every people in their separate languages would have thrown the gates of interpolation wide open, so that the miraculous quality of the Qur'an — that its original words remain perfectly protected — would not have survived intact.

Hence one language for the Book and for the Prophet ﷺ, with translations made and circulated afterwards, and the scholars of each people spreading his teachings among them in their own tongue. Thus, at least for all practical purposes of *daʿwah* (the call — inviting people to the message) and *tablīgh* (spreading the message), the difference of Arab and non-Arab was eliminated.

As for why *this* language: Maʿārif ul Qurʾān lists several reasons. Arabic is the official language of the heavens and the language of the angels; the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*) is in Arabic, as the Qur'an tells us — "Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an in the Preserved Tablet" (85:21–22); and Paradise, the real home of human beings, has Arabic as its language too. Cited here is a narration from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), found in the Muʿjam of al-Ṭabarānī, the Mustadrak of al-Ḥākim and the Shuʿab al-Īmān of al-Bayhaqī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Love Arabs for three reasons: that I am an Arab; and the Qur'an is in Arabic; and the language of the people of Paradise is Arabic." Its standing is disputed: in the Mustadrak, al-Ḥākim calls the narration Ṣaḥīḥ and the same rating appears in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, yet some ḥadīth experts have called it weak and not authentic, while Ibn Taymiyyah held that the subject of this ḥadīth is proven and cannot be rated any lesser than *ḥasan*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds further reasons: the inherent treasure of capabilities in the language itself; and a natural affinity Allah has gifted Muslims with towards Arabic, such that it is learnt easily as needed — which is why, in country after country the Ṣaḥābah reached, Arabic became the language of the whole country without any compulsion. Egypt, Syria and Iraq were not Arabic-speaking lands; today they are known as Arab countries.

There is also a narration reported in Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī that the language of Ādam (peace be upon him) in Jannah was Arabic, and that after he was sent to the earth and his repentance accepted, changes within Arabic itself gave birth to Syriac. This appears to support reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and others — collected by al-Suyūṭī in *al-Itqān* — that the original language of every Book Allah revealed was Arabic, which Jibrīl al-Amīn (peace be upon him) relayed to the prophets by translating it to them, while they conveyed it to their communities in their own language. On that view, the meanings of the other Scriptures are all from Allah while their words were changed; it is the unique feature of the Qur'an alone that, like its meanings, its words too are from Allah.

## "Then Allah lets stray whom He wills, and guides whom He wills"

Ibn Kathīr notes the sequence carefully: this comes **after the proof and evidence have been established** for the people. The messenger's task was to make the message clear; guidance and misguidance follow that explanation. *Al-ʿAzīz* — whatever He wills occurs, and whatever He does not will never occurs. *Al-Ḥakīm* — the All-Wise in His decisions, misleading those who deserve to be misled and guiding those who deserve guidance. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān ends on the same note: bringing someone onto the right path is beyond human control. That lies in the power of Allah alone. He is Mighty, and Wise.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the rule out of the opening ayah without softening it: there is only one way all the children of Ādam on this earth can be rescued from the evil layers of darkness into light — the Qur'an. The closer people come towards it, the more they find peace and security and relief in the present life and success at its best in the life to come; and the farther they remain from it, the more exposed they are to self-destruction in both.

So the passage asks three things of us. **Come near the Book** — recite it even in a season when you understand little, and do not stop at recitation, since understanding its meaning and acting on it is the basic purpose. **Take the three traits personally**, since Qurṭubī's principle turns them into a mirror: is the world weighing heavier than the Hereafter? Am I keeping anyone from the way of Allah? Am I reading the Qur'an to find my own opinion inside it? And **trust the road** — it leads to *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥamīd*, and one who takes it will never falter, provided he does not abandon it.

passages.title: Moses and the Days of Allah
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Having just described the Qur'an as a Book sent down so that the Prophet ﷺ might, in Ibn Kathir's words, "guide and call all people out of darkness into the light" (ayah 1), Allah now shows that this is nothing new: Musa (peace be upon him) was sent with exactly the same commission. What holds ayat 5–8 together is a single method of calling people back to Allah — remind them of *the Days of Allah*, His favours and His reckonings — and the two responses that method is designed to produce: patience and gratitude. The passage then opens gratitude out into a universal law (ayah 7), and finally strips away any illusion that our gratitude does Allah a favour (ayah 8).

## Ayah 5: the same mission, one prophet earlier

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 5 as a direct parallel. Allah says here, in his paraphrase: "Just as We sent you (O, Muhammad) and sent down to you the Book, in order that you might guide and call all people out of darkness into the light, We also sent Musa to the Children of Israel with Our Ayat." The command to Musa — "Bring out your people from darkness into light" — means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "call them to all that is good and righteous, in order that they might turn away from the darkness of ignorance and misguidance they indulged in, to the light of guidance and the enlightenment of faith."

**What are "Our signs"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two possibilities, both sound. *Āyāt* may mean the verses of the Torah, since the very purpose of that Book was to spread the light of truth. Or it may mean miracles — and Allah had particularly blessed Musa with nine, of which the staff turning into a snake and the hand becoming radiant are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an. Mujahid, cited by Ibn Kathir, said that this part of the ayah refers to the nine miracles. Musa was sent with miracles so open that, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, no sane human being who had once seen them could go on sticking to his earlier denial and disobedience.

**A subtle word choice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to scroll past. Here Musa is told to bring out *qawmaka*, "your people". But when this very subject was taken up in the first ayah of this same surah, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, the word *qawm* was not used; instead it was *an-nās*: "that you may take the people [that is, the human beings] out of darkness into the light." Musa's Divinely ordained mission as a prophet was for his people, the Bani Isra'il, and for others in Egypt, while the coming of the Prophet ﷺ was destined for the human beings of the entire world.

## "And remind them of the Days of Allah"

This is the heart of ayah 5, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the expression is used in two senses, both of which can apply here.

**First: days of judgement and upheaval.** *Ayyām* is simply the plural of *yawm*, "day". But "the Days of Allah" can denote the particular days in which some war or revolution occurred — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the battles of Badr, Uhud, al-Ahzab and Hunayn — or major events when punishment overtook past communities, pulverising and destroying nations and peoples known to be great and powerful. On this reading, the objective behind reminding people of such days is to warn them against the evil end of their disbelief.

**Second: days of favour.** The phrase equally means the blessings and favours of Allah. Ibn Kathir takes it this way and lists what Musa was to remind his people of: how Allah delivered them from the grip of Fir'awn and his injustice, tyranny and brutality; how He delivered them from their enemy, made a passage for them through the sea, shaded them with clouds, and sent down manna and quails. Mujahid, Qatadah and several others said this. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the shade of clouds over their heads in the wilderness of Tih — the desert of Sinai — the coming of *mann* and *salwā* as food, and the gushing forth of streams from stones when they needed water. It also notes that reminding someone who is basically good of the favour done by his benefactor is a form of constructive admonition, one that results in his being ashamed of his hostility and disobedience.

**Why both.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point here about the Qur'an's whole method of reform: the general pattern is to tie a command to the relevant ways of acting upon it. There are two ways of bringing the disobedient to the right path: putting the fear of punishment in their hearts, and reminding them of Divine blessings and favours so as to persuade them to be obedient to Allah. "Remind them of the Days of Allah" holds both keys at once.

## Who actually benefits: *ṣabbār shakūr*

Ayah 5 closes: "Truly, therein are Ayat for every patient, thankful (person)" — or, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering, "Surely, there are signs therein for every man of patience and gratitude." Here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, *āyāt* means signs and proofs: the Days of Allah — past events, whether of the punishment of the deniers of truth or of the blessings and favours of Allah — are full of the signs and proofs of the perfect power and eloquent wisdom of Allah.

Both descriptive words are what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls **forms of exaggeration** in Arabic — intensive forms. *Ṣabbār* is derived from *ṣabr* (patience) and means very patient and much enduring; *shakūr* is derived from *shukr* (gratitude) and means very grateful.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that these open signs and proofs are for the guidance of every observer, yet unfortunate indeed are the disbelievers, who simply do not care to ponder over them and so remain deprived of the benefit they would have derived. The people who really benefit are those who have combined in their person the best of patience and gratitude. Qatadah put it beautifully, as Ibn Kathir records: "Excellent is the servant who if he is tested, he observes patience, and if he is granted prosperity, he is thankful for it."

**Why these two, and no others?** Because between them they cover the whole of a life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, carried by al-Baihaqi, in which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: "Iman is composed of two parts, half of it is patience and the other half, gratitude." And `Abdullah ibn Mas`ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: patience is half of faith.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith which he records as being in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, all of the matter of the believer is amazing, for every decision that Allah decrees for him is good for him. If an affliction strikes him, he is patient and this is good for him; if a bounty is given to him, he is thankful and this is good for him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, for its part, cites a narration of Suhayb, may Allah be pleased with him, appearing in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim and the Musnad of Ahmad, in which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: "Every state of affairs for a true believer is nothing but good."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks why this is so. This is a quality of life no one else has been blessed with. If a true believer finds comfort, blessing, honour or recognition, he shows his gratitude before Allah, and that becomes a source of good for him in both worlds: in the material world the blessings Divinely promised increase and abide, while in the Hereafter one receives the greatest of rewards for gratitude. And if he is hit by pain or hardship, he observes patience — and because of his patience that hardship turns into ease and comfort for him. In this world that happens because the observers of patience are blessed with the company of Allah: "Surely, Allah is with those who observe patience" (8:46), and anyone who has Allah with him ultimately finds his hardship changed into comfort. As for the Hereafter, the reward for patience is limitless: "but then, paid in full to those who observe patience shall be their reward without reckoning" (39:10). The conclusion drawn: **no state in which a true believer is can be called bad.** A fall would make him rise again, and when hit by hardships he would emerge stronger and more polished. Faith is a priceless asset which transforms even the shocks of hardship into drafts of comfort.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays that Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) said he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say that Allah told `Isa (peace be upon him): He would create a community after him who, when they have what they desire and things turn out the way they want, would be grateful, and when they face an unpleasant situation against their wish and pleasure, would accept it as a source of reward from Allah and observe patience — and that this wisdom and forbearance would not be the outcome of their own personal wisdom and forbearance, but rather a certain part of Allah's own Wisdom and Forbearance bestowed upon them. (The source relays this through Mazhari without naming a collection.)

## Ayah 6: the memory Musa places before them

Ayah 6 is the worked example of the command in ayah 5; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this ayah carries the details of what was said earlier. Ibn Kathir: Allah states that Musa reminded his people about Allah's annals and days and of Allah's favours and bounties that He bestowed on them, when He saved them from Fir'awn and his people and the torment and disgrace they used to exert on them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture. Before Musa came, they were living as slaves of the Pharaoh — and even as slaves they were not treated humanely. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: they used to slaughter whomever they could find among their sons and let their females live. After the appearance of Musa, such was his *barakah* that Allah had them delivered from the punishing clutches of the Pharaoh. Allah delivered them from all this torment, says Ibn Kathir, and this is a great bounty indeed.

**"And in it was a tremendous trial from your Lord."** The word *balā'* can point in two directions, and Ibn Kathir reports both. It may mean the *favour* itself: "for He granted you (O Children of Israel) a great favor for which you are unable to perfectly thank Him." Or, as some scholars said, it may mean that what Fir'awn used to do to you was a tremendous trial. Ibn Kathir's own verdict: "Both meanings might be considered here and Allah knows best." He supports the double sense with another ayah: "And We tried them with good and evil in order that they might turn (to Allah)" (7:168). Ease tests as surely as hardship does — which is precisely why the two qualities named at the end of ayah 5 come as a pair.

## Ayah 7: the proclamation

"And when your Lord declared, 'If you express gratitude, I shall certainly give you more, and if you are ungrateful, then My punishment is severe.'"

**The word *ta'adhdhana*.** Ibn Kathir explains it as: proclaimed, and made known His promise to you. He adds that it is possible the ayah means your Lord has vowed and sworn by His might, grace and exaltedness — and cites the parallel usage in 7:167. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise takes the word in the sense of making known or announcing.

**What is being promised.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sense: if you are thankful for My blessings and do not waste them in acts of disobedience to Me and in deeds which have been prohibited, and try your best to mould your deeds to suit My pleasure, then I shall increase these blessings for you. And the increase could be in the amount and volume of the blessings, or in their continuity and permanence as well. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a report of Ibn Marduwayh from Ibn `Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A person who is blessed with the Taufiq to be grateful shall never be deprived of barakah and increase in blessings" — *tawfīq* meaning the enabling grace that Allah gives a servant to do what pleases Him.

**What ingratitude actually is.** Ibn Kathir glosses being thankless here as not being thankful for Allah's favours, covering and denying them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it concrete: the sum total of ungratefulness is that one spends out the blessings given by Allah in acts disobedient to Him and in things and ways which are impermissible, or that one is tardy in fulfilling what has been made obligatory. So ingratitude is not merely a failure to say "alhamdulillah"; it is using the gift against the Giver.

**And the punishment.** Ibn Kathir: "verily, My punishment is indeed severe" — by depriving you of the favour and punishing you for being unappreciative of it. He cites here a hadith, without naming its collection: "A servant might be deprived of a provision (that was written for him) because of a sin that he commits." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the worldly shape of that severity: it is possible that these blessings may be taken back all of a sudden, or that one falls into unwelcome circumstances which leave him unable to make use of the blessing — with punishment waiting in the Hereafter as well.

**The asymmetry.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an observation about the wording. On the side of gratitude, Allah promises reward and increase emphatically: *la-azīdannakum*, "I shall certainly give you more." But for the ungrateful it was not said, "I shall certainly punish you." What is given instead is a limited warning conveying the sense: "My punishment too, to whomsoever it reaches, is very severe." And in this interpretation, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, there is a hint that it is not necessary that every ungrateful person has to undergo punishment — the likelihood of forgiveness also exists.

## Ayah 8: "and all on earth together"

Musa closes: "If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich (free of all needs), Worthy of all praise."

Ibn Kathir: Allah does not need the gratitude of His servants, and He is worthy of all praise even if the disbelievers disbelieve in Him. He gathers the parallels: "If you disbelieve, then verily, Allah is not in need of you" (39:7), and "So they disbelieved and turned away. But Allah was not in need (of them). And Allah is Rich (free of all needs), Worthy of all praise" (64:6).

The two names at the end of the ayah say two different things. **Al-Ghaniyy** — the Rich, free of all needs: as Ibn Kathir says, Allah does not need the gratitude of His servants; as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, He needs no praise or gratitude for Himself, He is Independent, He is beyond that. **Al-Ḥamīd** — Worthy of all praise: He is worthy of all praise even if the disbelievers disbelieve in Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: He is intrinsically Praised and deserving of praise; if you do not praise Him, the angels do, all of them, and so does every particle of this universe.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here what Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, that Abu Dharr said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that his Lord, the Exalted and Most Honoured, said: "O My servants. If the first and the last among you, mankind and Jinns among you, had the heart of the most pious and righteous man among you, that will not increase my kingdom in the least. O My servants! If the first and the last among you, mankind and the Jinns among you, had the heart of the most wicked man among you, that will not decrease My kingdom in the least. O My servants! If the first and the last among you, the mankind and Jinns among you, stood in one flat area and each asked me (what they wish), and I gave each one of them what they asked, that will not decrease My kingdom except by that which the needle carries (of water) when inserted in the ocean."

**The conclusion Musa is driving at.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: whatever good there is in gratitude, that is for you alone. When Allah asks you to be grateful, there is no gain for Him in it; in fact it is His infinite mercy reaching out to you, in your own interest. Should you — or, for that matter, all the inhabitants of the earth — become ungrateful, it is not going to cause any loss to Allah. Ayat 7 and 8 therefore fit together perfectly: the One who promises to increase you for thanking Him is the very One who needs nothing from your thanks.

## Living it

**The substance of *shukr*,** as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it: that one should not spend out the blessings given by Allah in what is Haram, in things which are not permitted, and in being disobedient to Him; that one should also show gratitude by saying so; and that one should model and channel one's deeds so that they come to be in accordance with His good pleasure. That, more than any feeling, is where gratitude is decided.

**The substance of *ṣabr*,** likewise: that we should not worry about what comes to be against our wishes, taste or temperament; that we avoid being ungrateful in what we say or do; that we keep hoping for the mercy of Allah in this mortal life; and that we remain certain of the great reward of patience due in the Hereafter as well.

**And the practice of ayah 5 itself:** remind yourself, and those you are responsible for, of the Days of Allah — the days He rescued, and the days He called nations to account. Not as history for its own sake, but because, as ayah 5 says, in those days are signs. The ones who truly benefit from them are those who have combined in themselves the best of patience and gratitude.

passages.title: Past nations and their messengers' patience
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are one scene. Ibn Kathir describes the passage as Allah narrating to us "the arguments that ensued between the disbelievers and their Messengers" — a single running exchange rather than four separate lessons. It opens with a question put to the hearers about the nations that came before, and then the conversation itself unfolds: the people's flat refusal, the messengers' question back, the people's counter-demand, the messengers' answer, and their closing stand of patience and reliance on Allah. The last word in the scene belongs to the messengers.

## Where the scene begins

Ayah 8 ended with Musa (peace be upon him) telling his people that if they and everyone on earth turned ungrateful, it would cost Allah nothing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the point out: Allah needs no praise or gratitude for Himself. He is Independent. He is intrinsically Praised and deserving of praise. If you do not praise Him, the angels do — all of them — and so does every particle of this universe. So whatever good there is in gratitude is for you alone. When Allah asks you to be grateful, there is no gain for Him in it; it is "His infinite mercy reaching out to you in your interest."

Ayah 9 then turns the camera. If ingratitude harms only the ungrateful, look at what became of those who chose it.

## "Has the news not reached you?"

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah narrated to this Ummah — the followers of Muhammad ﷺ — the stories of the people of Nuh, of ʿĀd and Thamud, and of other ancient nations that belied their Messengers. It is put as a question, but the question carries its own answer inside it: the report *has* come. The evidence from history is not missing.

**"...and those after them? None knows them but Allah."** Three nations are named, and then the list is closed. Only Allah knows the count of these nations. Ibn Kathir records here a striking comment: Ibn Isḥāq reported that ʿAmr bin Maymūn said that ʿAbdullāh said about the words *"None knows them but Allah"* — **"The genealogists utter lies."** Ibn Kathir adds that this is why ʿUrwah bin az-Zubayr said, "We did not find anyone who knows the forefathers of Maʿdd bin ʿAdnān."

The Qurʼān names what it names, and then hands the rest back to Allah. A believer is not asked to fill in what Allah kept to Himself.

**"To them came their Messengers with clear proofs."** *Bayyināt* — Ibn Kathir glosses it as evidences and plain, tremendous proofs and signs. Hold that in mind, because everything that follows in this scene happens *after* the proofs arrived, not before them.

## "They put their hands in their mouths"

The Arabic *fa-raddū aydiyahum fī afwāhihim* is one of the more discussed images in the sūrah, and Ibn Kathir lays out the readings side by side rather than flattening them into one. The views he reports:

- **They gestured toward the Messengers' mouths** — asking them to stop calling them to Allah.
- **They placed their own hands on their own mouths** in denial of the Messengers.
- **They simply did not answer** the call of the Messengers.
- **They were biting their hands in rage.**
- **Mujāhid, Muḥammad bin Kaʿb and Qatādah** said it means they belied the Messengers and refuted their call with their mouths.

Ibn Kathir then gives his own preference: "I say that Mujāhid's Tafsīr is supported by the completion of the narrative" — because the ayah itself finishes the sentence with what came out of their mouths: *"Verily, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and we are really in grave doubt as to that to which you invite us."* The image of hands and mouths is explained by the very words that follow it.

Alongside this, Ibn Kathir preserves a report of a different tone: al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "When they heard Allah's Word, they were amazed and placed their hands on their mouths." That reading is worth pausing on. They were *struck* by what they heard — and still said, in Ibn ʿAbbās's rendering, "We do not believe what you brought us, and have strong doubt in its authenticity." Being amazed by the truth and submitting to it are not the same thing.

Notice also how their sentence is arranged. The disbelief is stated first — *"we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"* — and the doubt second, which the ayah qualifies as *grave* doubt (*shakkin murīb*).

## The messengers answer with a question

**"Is there any doubt about Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth?"** The messengers do not begin by defending themselves; they go to the foundation. Ibn Kathir specifies what the doubt concerns: **His Lordship and His having the exclusive right to be worshipped alone**, He being the only Creator of all creatures — for truly, none besides Allah is worthy of worship, alone, without partners.

And here Ibn Kathir makes an observation with a long reach: **"Most nations were, and still are, affirming the existence of the Creator, but they call upon intermediaries besides Him whom they think will benefit them or bring them closer to Allah."** Most of these nations did not deny that a Creator exists. Their failure was in the second half — directing their calling-upon to go-betweens, on the theory that these would bring benefit or shorten the distance to Allah. The messengers' question therefore lands not merely on *whether* Allah is, but on whether any room is left beside the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

**"He calls you that He may forgive you of your sins and give you respite for a term appointed."** Ibn Kathir distributes this over the two homes: forgiveness of sins **in the Hereafter**, and respite **in this worldly life**. He supports it with Allah's words elsewhere: *"Seek the forgiveness of your Lord, and turn to Him in repentance, that He may grant you good enjoyment, for a term appointed, and bestow His abounding grace to every owner of grace"* (Hūd 11:3).

Read the wording carefully. The messengers say **He calls you**, and the purpose clause that follows is entirely in the hearers' favour: so that He may forgive, so that He may grant time. This is the same shape Maʿārif ul Qurʼān drew from ayah 8 — the summons is mercy reaching toward you, not a levy taken from you.

## The goalposts move

Ibn Kathir marks the turn precisely: "their nations went on arguing against their prophethood, **after they had to submit to the first evidence** (that Allah Alone created everything)." Unable to hold the line on the Creator, they fall back to a second line — the messenger himself:

- *"You are no more than human beings like us!"* — meaning, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase, so why should we follow you just because you say so, even though we did not witness a miracle by your hands?
- *"You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship."* — they name what they are defending.
- *"Then bring us a clear authority"* — *sulṭān mubīn*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and exact: **a miracle of our choice.**

That gloss is the key to the whole demand. Proof had already come — *bayyināt*, ayah 9. What is being asked for now is proof on their own terms, of their own selection.

## "We are only human, but..."

The messengers concede the premise without conceding the claim. Ibn Kathir: they affirm that truly, they were only human beings like their nations — **"but Allah bestows His grace to whom He wills of His servants,"** with prophethood and messengership, which is **His choice**. Being human was never an argument against being sent; the sending is a favour Allah places where He wills.

Then the demand for a custom miracle is answered on two levels:

- *"It is not ours to bring you an authority"* — Ibn Kathir adds the crucial qualifier: **according to your choice.**
- *"except by the permission of Allah"* — Ibn Kathir: after we beg Him and He provides us with a miracle.

So the door is not shut; it simply is not theirs to open. A messenger asks; Allah gives. This is a clean statement of the boundary between the servant and the Lord: the messengers, of all people, say plainly that they do not carry signs at their own disposal.

**"And in Allah alone let the believers put their trust."** Ibn Kathir: in **all their affairs**. The sentence arrives exactly where it is needed. Having just said they cannot supply what is being demanded, they do not fall silent — they turn to *tawakkul*, reliance on Allah.

## The closing stand

**"And why should we not put our trust in Allah, while He indeed has guided us in our ways?"** This is *tawakkul* with a reason attached. Ibn Kathir supplies it: after He had guided us to the best, most clear and plain way. Their trust rests on what Allah has already done with them, not on a hopeful mood.

**"And we shall certainly bear with patience all the hurt you may cause us."** Ibn Kathir specifies the kind of hurt meant: **foolish actions and abusive statements.** Not only persecution in the dramatic sense — mockery, insults, the daily contempt of people who have decided you are ridiculous.

Two things are worth noticing about where this sits in the conversation. First, it is what the messengers say when cornered: they have been called liars, told they are nothing special, and challenged to perform on command. What they answer with is neither a threat nor a defence of their own dignity — it is a promise to endure. Second, the passage does not leave endurance standing on its own. Straight after the promise to bear the hurt comes the closing line.

**"And in Allah alone let those who trust put their trust."** The scene ends by repeating the instruction that closed ayah 11 — there addressed to *the believers* (**al-muʼminūn**), here to *those who trust* (**al-mutawakkilūn**). Reliance on Allah is the last word spoken in the whole exchange.

## Living it

- **Do not wait for proof you have already been given.** Ayah 9 makes the point twice: the news *has* reached you, and the messengers came *with clear proofs*. In this scene the refusal comes after the evidence, not for want of it.
- **Test where your calling-upon actually goes.** Ibn Kathir's note that nations affirmed the Creator yet still called on intermediaries "to bring them closer to Allah" is the sharpest self-check in the passage. What these nations lacked was not belief that a Creator exists; it was worship directed to Allah alone, without partners.
- **Stop setting the terms.** "Bring us a clear authority" meant, in Ibn Kathir's gloss, *a miracle of our choice*. The same shape appears whenever we attach private conditions to belief — I will commit when this duʿāʼ is answered, when this hardship lifts. The messengers' answer stands: a sign is not theirs to produce on request; it comes by Allah's permission.
- **Answer contempt with endurance.** The hurt named here is foolish behaviour and abusive words, and what the messengers offer in reply is patience and reliance on Allah rather than retaliation.
- **Anchor your trust in what Allah has already done.** *"Why should we not put our trust in Allah, while He indeed has guided us in our ways?"* Ibn Kathir reads that as: after He guided us to the best, most clear and plain way. If He has given you that, reason forward from it when smaller things are uncertain.

passages.title: Tyrants threaten the messengers and are destroyed
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are one scene played out from beginning to end: a threat, a promise, an appeal for judgment, and the sentence. In ayah 13 the disbelieving nations issue their ultimatum to the messengers; in the same breath Allah answers with a counter-decree (13–14); in ayah 15 the matter is put before Allah for judgment; and in 16–17 we are shown, in unhurried detail, what the losing side receives. The passage is about who actually owns the land, and who actually decides an outcome.

## Ayah 13: "our land" and "our religion"

Ibn Kathir opens by noting that this is not one incident but a pattern: Allah narrates to us how the disbelieving nations threatened their messengers with expulsion from their land and banishment. He gathers the parallels:

- The people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: "We shall certainly drive you out from our town, O Shu'ayb, and those who have believed with you" (7:88) — note that the believers are threatened alongside the prophet.
- The people of Lut, peace be upon him: "Drive out the family of Lut from your city" (27:56).

The ultimatum in ayah 13 has two halves, and both are worth pausing over. In Ibn Kathir's rendering it runs: "Surely, we shall drive you out of our land, or you shall return to our religion." The first half is territorial — *arḍinā*, "**our** land." The tyrant speaks as though the earth were a deed in his pocket. The second is a demand of conformity: come back to our religion. Exile or capitulation; the sentence itself offers no third option. That is what makes it a tyrant's offer rather than an argument — nothing in it engages with whether the message is true.

## The same threat reached the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir brings the pattern right up to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah says of the idolaters of Quraysh: "And verily, they were about to frighten you so much as to drive you out from the land. But in that case they would not have stayed after you, except for a little while" (17:76) — the expulsion and the expellers' own removal are named in a single sentence. And the fuller version of their scheming: "And when the disbelievers plotted against you to imprison you, or to kill you, or to expel you out; they were plotting and Allah too was plotting; and Allah is the Best of those who plot" (8:30). Three plans lay on their table. The ayah sets all of it against Allah's own planning, and closes by naming Him the Best of those who plot.

So when a believer reads ayah 13 today, he is not only reading ancient history. He is reading a pattern the Qur'an itself traces from nation to nation, right down to the Prophet ﷺ.

## Ayat 13–14: the answer comes as revelation

Look closely at how Allah replies: *fa-awḥā ilayhim rabbuhum* — "So their Lord revealed to them." The answer is not delivered to the tyrants as a debating point. It is delivered privately to the messengers, as revelation, as reassurance. The people making the threats are not even addressed. And what is revealed comes as two declarations:

1. **"Truly, We shall destroy the wrongdoers"** — the threat is answered at its source.
2. **"And indeed, We shall make you dwell in the land after them"** — and this is the exquisite part. They said "**our** land." Allah replies that you will live in it after they are gone. Not a different land, not compensation elsewhere. The very ground they claimed as theirs will hold the feet of the people they wanted to drive off it.

## How this was fulfilled in the life of the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir traces the promise into the life of the Prophet ﷺ himself, and this is the passage's most illuminating context. Allah gave victory and aid to His Messenger ﷺ after he emigrated from Makkah and gathered around him followers, supporters and soldiers who fought in the cause of Allah, the Exalted. Allah kept granting His Messenger ﷺ more dominance until He opened for him Makkah — the very city that had sought to expel him. Allah gave him dominance over it, even when his enemies from Makkah and the rest of the people of the earth disliked it. Soon after, people began embracing the religion of Allah in large crowds, and in a very short time Allah's Word and religion became high over all other religions, from the eastern and western parts of the world.

Sit with the sequence. The man driven out is the one to whom that same city is opened. Ibn Kathir tells this history and then says, "Hence Allah's statement," and quotes 14:13–14. For him, this is what the promise looks like once it has come true.

## Not a one-off favour but a standing decree

Ibn Kathir stacks up the ayat that make this a fixed word of Allah rather than a special mercy for one prophet:

- "And, verily, Our Word has gone forth of old for Our servants, the Messengers, that they verily, would be made triumphant, and that Our hosts! They verily, would be the victors" (37:171–173).
- "Allah has decreed: 'Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious. Verily, Allah is All-Powerful, All-Mighty'" (58:21).
- "And indeed We have written in Az-Zabur after Adh-Dhikr that My righteous servants shall inherit the land" (21:105) — written down in earlier scripture too.

And two ayat that name the price of that inheritance. Musa, peace be upon him, told his people: "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Verily, the earth is Allah's. He gives it as a heritage to whom He wills of His servants: and the (blessed) end is for those who have Taqwa" (7:128). The earth is Allah's — that single clause dismantles the tyrant's phrase "our land." And of the Children of Israel: "And We made the people who were considered weak to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof which We have blessed. And the fair Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel, **because of their endurance**. And We destroyed completely all the great works and buildings which Fir'awn and his people erected" (7:137). Fir'awn's monuments went; the ones counted weak inherited. The stated reason is their endurance.

## The clause that qualifies the promise (end of ayah 14)

"This is for him who fears standing before Me and also fears My threat." Ibn Kathir explains: this is for the one who fears standing before Him on the Day of Resurrection and fears His warnings and torment. The promise of dwelling in the land is not a blank cheque issued to anyone who carries a religious label. It is tied to a particular interior state — a heart that lives with the awareness of that standing.

Allah pairs these two outcomes elsewhere in exactly this way: "Then for him who transgressed all bounds, and preferred the life of this world, verily, his abode will be Hellfire. But as for him who feared standing before his Lord, and restrained himself from impure evil desires and lusts. Verily, Paradise will be his abode" (79:37–41). And: "But for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there will be two Gardens" (55:46). Notice how the first of those passages pairs the fear of that standing directly with restraining the self from desire. The fear is not a passing mood; in the ayah's own wording it shows itself as restraint.

## Ayah 15: who sought the judgment

*Wa-stafataḥū* — Ibn Kathir renders it "And they sought victory and help." The classical scholars differed over who "they" are, and the difference is instructive rather than troubling:

- **The messengers**, who sought the help and victory of their Lord over their nations — this is the view Ibn Kathir reports from 'Abdullah bin 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.
- **The nations themselves**, invoking Allah's victory against their own heads — the view of 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam. Ibn Kathir cites what some idolaters said: "O Allah! If this (Qur'an) is indeed the truth (revealed) from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment" (8:32). They asked for it by name.

Ibn Kathir's own judgment is that **both meanings may be intended at once**, and he points to Badr: there the idolaters of Quraysh invoked Allah against themselves, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked Him for victory and support. Allah's word to the idolaters afterwards: "(O disbelievers) if you ask for a judgment, now has the judgment come unto you; and if you cease (to do wrong), it will be better for you" (8:19). You asked for a judgment. Here is the judgment. Ibn Kathir closes the discussion with the scholar's honesty: *Allah knows best.*

## The tyrant's complete loss

Of *wa khāba kullu jabbārin ʿanīd*, Ibn Kathir gives the meaning plainly: "and every obstinate, arrogant dictator was brought to a complete loss and destruction" — those who were arrogant and rebelled against the truth. Not merely wrong, but wrong and immovable.

The Qur'an describes the same figure being taken away: "(Allah will say to the angels): 'Both of you throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever — hinderer of good, transgressor, doubter, who set up another deity with Allah. Then both of you cast him in the severe torment'" (50:24–26).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a statement of the Prophet ﷺ — the source before us does not name the collection it comes from — that on the Day of Resurrection Jahannam (Hellfire) will be brought and it will call the creatures, saying: "I was given the responsibility of every rebellious tyrant." The Fire itself announces its assignment.

Then Ibn Kathir draws the thread of the passage together: every tyrant has earned utter demise and loss when the Prophets invoked Allah, the Mighty, the Able, for victory. **Every** one — no exceptions are being carved out for the impressive ones.

## Ayat 16–17: what "loss" actually means

Ayah 15 said he lost. Ayat 16–17 refuse to leave that as an abstraction.

**"In front of him is Hell."** Ibn Kathir explains that Jahannam is in front of every obstinate tyrant, awaiting him, and that he will reside in it forever on the Day of Return; he will be brought to it in the morning and the afternoon until the Day of the Call. Notice that the phrase Ibn Kathir renders "in front of him" opens ayah 16 and then returns at the very end of ayah 17 — Hell in front of him, and, in front of him again, a great torment. Every direction he faces is forward into worse.

**The drink.** "And he will be made to drink boiling, festering water." Ibn Kathir says that in the Fire his only drink will be from *Ḥamīm* and *Ghassāq* — the former very hot, the latter very cold and rotten, as in "This is so! Then let them taste it — Hamim and Ghassaq. And other (torments) of similar kind all together!" (38:57–58). Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said this festering water is made of pus and blood. Elsewhere: "And be given to drink boiling water so that it cuts up their bowels" (47:15), and "And if they ask for help, they will be granted water like boiling oil, that will scald their faces" (18:29) — help asked for, help granted, and the granting is the punishment.

**"He will sip it unwillingly."** Ibn Kathir's comment on the phrase is that he will hate to drink this water, but he will be forced to sip it; he will refuse, until the angel strikes him with an iron bar — "And for them are hooked rods of iron" (22:21). Then: "and he will find great difficulty in swallowing it down his throat" — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, that he will hate to swallow it because of its awful taste, colour and unbearable heat or coldness. The man who in ayah 13 issued ultimatums no longer controls what enters his own mouth.

**"And death will come to him from every side, yet he will not die."** Ibn Kathir: his organs, limbs and entire body will suffer pain because of this drink. 'Amr bin Maymun bin Mahran commented: "Every bone, nerve and blood vessel." Ad-Dahhak reported that Ibn 'Abbas explained the phrase this way: all types of torment that Allah will punish him with on the Day of Resurrection in the fire of Jahannam will come to him carrying death — *if he were to die*. But he will not die, because Allah said: "Neither will it affect them that they die nor shall its torment be lightened for them" (35:36). Death arrives from every direction as a visitor who never actually enters. He will not die; he will instead receive eternal punishment and torment.

**"And in front of him, will be a great torment."** Even in that condition, Ibn Kathir says, he will still suffer another severe type of torment, more severe and painful than the one before it, harsher and more bitter. He then gathers the descriptions of the tree of Zaqqum — "Verily, it is a tree that springs out of the bottom of Hellfire, the shoots of its fruits stalks are like the heads of Shayatin; Truly, they will eat thereof and fill their bellies therewith. Then on top of that they will be given boiling water to drink so that it becomes a mixture. Then thereafter, verily, their return is to the flaming fire of Hell" (37:64–68) — and concludes that they will either be eating from the Zaqqum, drinking the Ḥamīm, or being tormented in the Fire, again and again. At which point Ibn Kathir breaks off to say what any honest reader feels: *we seek refuge with Allah from all of this.*

He notes that the punishment they receive is of different kinds, repeated in various types and forms that only Allah the Exalted knows, **as just recompense** — and then seals the whole passage with the ayah that guards it from being misread as cruelty: **"And your Lord is not at all unjust to (His) slaves"** (41:46). This is recompense, measured exactly.

## Living it

**If you are on the receiving end of the threat.** The passage speaks to people being told to leave their homes or abandon their faith. Its comfort is not that the pressure will be light, but that Allah delivered His verdict to His messengers by revelation — privately, before the tyrants were addressed at all. Musa's instruction to a crushed people remains the practical instruction: seek help in Allah, and be patient. The Children of Israel inherited east and west, and the ayah names the reason: *because of their endurance*.

**Do not be impressed by the tyrant's moment.** Ibn Kathir's conclusion is not that the tyrant may lose but that he has already earned utter demise and loss. What looks like strength is standing under a verdict already recorded.

**Check the description, not the throne.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *jabbār ʿanīd* — those who were arrogant and rebelled against the truth — describes a character before it describes an office. The ayah says *every*. A man with no power at all can hold the same posture in a small argument he knows he has lost.

**Hold on to the condition in ayah 14.** The promise belongs to "him who fears standing before Me and also fears My threat." That fear is what the whole passage is built to produce — which is why 16 and 17 are so unsparing, and why they end on "And your Lord is not at all unjust to (His) slaves." They are a mercy in the form of a warning, delivered while there is still time to heed it. And they end where Ibn Kathir himself ended: *we seek refuge with Allah from all of this.*

passages.title: Deeds like ashes, and a creation He could replace
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form a single argument in two moves. In ayah 18 Allah gives a parable for what becomes of a lifetime of effort built on rejecting Him: works like ashes, in a strong wind, on a stormy day. In ayat 19 and 20 He points to the heavens and the earth, and says that if He wills He can remove you and bring a new creation in your place — and that this, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "is not hard or impossible for Allah to do that. Rather, it is easy for Him."

## Ayah 18: works like ashes, on a stormy day

Notice how the ayah is framed. The parable is of **the people** — "the parable of those who disbelieved in their Lord" — and what the picture shows you is **their works**: their works "are as ashes, on which the wind blows furiously on a stormy day; they shall not be able to get aught of what they have earned. That is the straying, far away (from the right path)" (Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah).

Ibn Kathir sets the scene precisely. This is "a parable that Allah has given for the deeds and actions of the disbelievers who worshipped others besides Him and rejected His Messengers, thus building their acts on groundless basis. Their actions vanished from them when they were most in need of their rewards."

Then he places you at the moment the parable is about — the Day of Judgment, "when they will seek their rewards from Allah the Exalted." And here is the most chilling line in his comment: **"They used to think that they had something, but they will find nothing."** The loss is not only the loss itself; it is the shock of discovering it, at the one moment when there is nothing left to be done about it.

**These are their good deeds.** That deserves underlining, because it is easy to misread the ayah as being about wickedness. Ibn Kathir says plainly: "They will not earn rewards for any of the good works they performed during this life, except what they can preserve of ashes during a day of strong wind."

Sit with that last phrase. Ibn Kathir does not tell you how much a person can preserve of ashes on a day of strong wind. He leaves the picture standing and lets you answer.

## Three more pictures of the same loss

Ibn Kathir gathers other ayat that draw the same thing in different images, and reading them together makes the point land:

- **"And We shall turn to whatever deeds they did, and We shall make such deeds as scattered floating particles of dust"** (25:23) — the deeds are not overlooked. They are attended to, and then scattered.
- **"The parable of what they spend in this world is that of a wind which is extremely cold; it struck the harvest of a people who did wrong against themselves and destroyed it. Allah wronged them not, but they wronged themselves"** (3:117) — a whole harvest, killed where it stood. And the ayah itself closes off the obvious objection: this is not Allah wronging them. They wronged themselves.
- **"His parable is that of a smooth rock on which is a little dust; on it falls heavy rain which leaves it bare. They are not able to do anything with what they have earned"** (2:264).

That third one repays a second look, because its closing clause is the closing clause of our own ayah. Ayah 18: "they shall not be able to get aught of what they have earned." Ayah 2:264: "They are not able to do anything with what they have earned." The same verdict, attached to two different images — ash carried off by wind, and dust washed off rock.

It is also worth noticing how the ayah Ibn Kathir quotes here opens, in its own words: **"O you who believe! Do not render in vain your Sadaqah (charity) by reminders of your generosity or by injury, like him who spends his wealth to be seen of men."**

## "That is the straying, far away"

The ayah closes: "That is the straying, far away from the right path." Ibn Kathir explains it as "their work and deeds were not based on firm, correct grounds, and thus, they lost their rewards when they needed them the most."

That gloss is worth pausing on, because it tells you where the straying actually lies. These were people who had performed good works — Ibn Kathir says so. What was missing, in his words, was firm and correct grounds beneath them: they had "worshipped others besides Him and rejected His Messengers, thus building their acts on groundless basis." The problem named here is the foundation, not the quantity.

## Ayah 19: look, and reason from what you see

The passage now shifts its footing entirely, from parable to evidence: **"Do you not see that Allah has created the heavens and the earth with truth?"**

The ayah is put as a question — and Ibn Kathir answers it by listing what there is to see. He heads this section **"Proof that Resurrection occurs after Death."** Allah, he says, "affirms His ability to resurrect the bodies on the Day of Resurrection, stating that He has created the heavens and earth which are stronger than the creation of man."

Then he asks you to actually look at the two of them. Is not He who is able to create the heavens — "high, wide and strongly built, which include in them the planets and stars and the various heavenly objects and clear signs"? Is not He who created "this earth with all what it contains of land, valleys, mountains, deserts, green fields, barren lands, seas and various shapes, benefits, species and colors of trees, plants and animals"?

The reasoning is one of scale: the stronger creation has already been done, in front of your eyes. Ibn Kathir cites **"Do they not see that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, He surely, is able to do all things"** (46:33), and the passage in Sūrah Yā Sīn where a man "puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!'" (36:77-83) — a man whom Allah "created ... from Nutfah (drop of sperm)", standing forth, in that same passage's words, "as an open opponent."

## "If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation"

This is the sentence that should stop a reader. Ibn Kathir's explanation: it "means, it is not hard or impossible for Allah to do that. Rather, it is easy for Him, that if you defy His order, He takes you away and brings in your place another creation who is unlike you."

He then lines up the parallels across the Qur'an, and each one adds a shade:

- **"O mankind! It is you who stand in need of Allah. But Allah is Rich, Worthy of all praise. If He willed, He could destroy you and bring about a new creation. And that is not hard for Allah"** (35:15-17) — the same sentence as ours, but prefaced by the ayah's own diagnosis: the neediness runs one way only.
- **"And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people and they will not be your likes"** (47:38) — the exchange is tied to turning away.
- **"O you who believe! Whoever from among you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring a people whom He will love and they will love Him"** (5:54) — and notice how the replacement is described here. Not merely as other people, but in the language of love running both ways: He will love them, and they will love Him.
- **"If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others. And Allah is Ever All-Potent over that"** (4:133).

## Ayah 20: "and that is not difficult for Allah at all"

Ibn Kathir does not stop at the negative. He says it "is not hard or impossible for Allah to do that" — and then adds: **"Rather, it is easy for Him."** The denial of difficulty is turned into a positive statement of ease.

And he has already put a supporting phrase in front of us. In 46:33, quoted a few lines earlier, Allah describes Himself as the One who created the heavens and the earth and "was not wearied by their creation."

Something else follows from where Ibn Kathir places these two ayat. He reads 19-20 as proof that resurrection occurs after death — while ayah 18 has already shown us the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, "when they will seek their rewards from Allah the Exalted." So the passage gives both halves at once: the certainty that the Day comes, and the scene of what is found there.

## The thread running underneath: Allah's independence

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a theme from earlier in the sūrah that this passage is standing on. In ayah 8, Mūsā (peace be upon him) tells his people: "If you are ungrateful, you and all those on earth, then, Allah is free of all needs, worthy of every praise." The commentary explains that even if they, "or, for that matter, all inhabitants of the earth become ungrateful to Allah Taʿālā, it is not going to cause any loss to Allah Taʿālā. As for Him, He needs no praise or gratitude for Himself. He is Independent. He is beyond that. He is intrinsically Praised and deserving of praise. If you do not praise Him, the angels do, all of them, and so does every particle of this universe."

And then the conclusion that turns the whole thing warm: "whatever good there is in gratitude, that is for you alone. Therefore, when you are asked to be grateful by Allah Taʿālā, there is no gain for Him in doing so. In fact, it is His infinite mercy reaching out to you in your interest."

Put that beside our three ayat and they click into place. Ayah 18: what was lost was *their* reward, needed by *them*, at the moment *they* most needed it — the loss falls entirely on the one who built on nothing. Ayat 19-20: "It is you who stand in need of Allah. But Allah is Rich, Worthy of all praise." Everything in the relationship that benefits, benefits **you**. Even the warning about ashes is, on Maʿārif's reading of gratitude, mercy reaching out in your interest.

## Living it

**Check the base, not just the total.** The people in ayah 18 were not idle — Ibn Kathir speaks of "the good works they performed during this life." What they lacked, in his words, was firm and correct grounds: they had "worshipped others besides Him and rejected His Messengers." The question the ayah presses is not how much has been built, but what it was built on.

**Guard the deeds you have already done.** The ayah Ibn Kathir brings here says it in its own words: "O you who believe! Do not render in vain your Sadaqah (charity) by reminders of your generosity or by injury." That instruction is addressed to believers, about charity they have actually given. The reminder of one's own generosity, and injury to the person helped, are named there as things that render a deed vain.

**Drop the assumption that we are indispensable.** "It is you who stand in need of Allah. But Allah is Rich, Worthy of all praise" (35:15). "And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people" (47:38). Yet the exchange in 5:54 is described as a people "whom He will love and they will love Him" — so what is being described is not the end of the religion, but the end of a particular set of carriers.

**Make gratitude a habit and know who it is for.** On Maʿārif's reading, being asked to be thankful is itself an act of kindness towards us: "whatever good there is in gratitude, that is for you alone."

**And answer the question ayah 19 asks.** "Do you not see...?" Ibn Kathir spells out what there is to see: heavens "high, wide and strongly built," the planets and stars, and an earth of "land, valleys, mountains, deserts, green fields, barren lands, seas and various shapes, benefits, species and colors of trees, plants and animals." He is not pointing at anything hidden. He is pointing at what is already in front of us.

passages.title: Mutual blame in the Fire, peace in the Gardens
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat show the Day when the ties built on falsehood come apart. Ayah 21 gives the first exchange of that Day — followers turning on the leaders they once obeyed. Ayah 22 gives the second — Shaytan standing up to disown his own followers. Then ayah 23 turns to the people of faith, brought into Gardens where the greeting is "Peace."

What holds the three together is that they are three speeches. Two are recrimination; the third is *salam*. Ibn Kathir marks the same division when he says that Allah "mentioned the final destination of the miserable ones... then He mentioned the final destination of the happy ones."

## "They will all appear before Allah" (21)

Ibn Kathir explains **وَبَرَزُوا** — *they shall appear* — as meaning that all the creatures, "the wicked and the righteous among them, will appear before Allah the One, the Irresistible." And he adds the detail that makes the scene: "They will be gathered on a flat plain that does not have anything those present could use for cover."

Hold that picture. Everyone brought out before Allah, on ground that offers nothing to hide behind.

## Speech one: the followers and those who made themselves great

Ibn Kathir names the two parties precisely. **الضعفاء**, "the weak," are "the followers who used to obey their chiefs, leaders and notables." **الذين استكبروا**, "those who were arrogant," are those "who rebelled against worshipping Allah alone without partners and obeying the Messengers." So this is not strong versus weak in any worldly sense. Each group is defined by what it did with Allah's command: one rebelled against worshipping Him alone and against obeying the Messengers; the other gave its obedience to chiefs, leaders and notables.

The followers say, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase, "we obeyed your orders and implemented them" — and then the question that is really a reproach: "can you prevent any of Allah's torment from striking us **as you used to promise and vow to us**?" The relationship rested on a guarantee. Now the guarantee is called in.

**"Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you."** Ibn Kathir unpacks the leaders' reply: "but the statement of our Lord shall come to pass concerning us, and the destiny that He has appointed for us and you shall come true; the word of punishment shall befall the disbelievers."

Read this for what it is — the reported speech of the ruined leaders themselves. Set it beside what the very next ayah has Shaytan say to the same crowd: *blame yourselves*, and Ibn Kathir's gloss on why — "because it is your fault for defying the proofs and following me in the falsehood that I called you to."

Then the collapse: **"It makes no difference to us whether we rage, or bear these torments with patience; there is no place of refuge for us."** Ibn Kathir: "we have no means of escape from what we are in, whether we face it with patience or grief."

That line deserves a pause. Two opposite responses to suffering — raging against it and bearing it — and there they arrive at exactly the same place. Even the choice between them has stopped changing anything.

## Where is this conversation taking place?

Ibn Kathir gives his own judgement: "it appears that this conversation will occur in the Fire after they enter it." He supports it from parallel ayat — 40:47–48, where "when they will dispute in the Fire" the arrogant reply, "We are all together in this Fire! Verily, Allah has judged between His servants"; 7:38–39, where "every time a new nation enters, it curses its sister nation," the last blaming the first, and the first answering, "You were not better than us, so taste the torment for what you used to earn"; and 33:67–68, "Our Lord! Verily, we obeyed our chiefs and our great ones, and they misled us from the way."

He then adds that the disbelievers will also dispute on the Day of Gathering, citing 34:31–33 — the weak say, "Had it not been for you, we certainly have been believers"; the arrogant answer, "Did we keep you back from guidance after it had come to you? Nay, but you were wrongdoers"; and the weak come back with, "Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day."

Put together: the blaming runs at the Gathering and on inside the Fire — and in none of these scenes does it lighten anyone's share. In 7:38–39 the request for a double torment for the misleaders is answered, "For each one there is double, but you know not." In 40:48 the answer is simply, "We are all together in this Fire."

## Speech two: Shaytan takes the stand (22)

Timing is everything here: **"when the matter has been decided."** Ibn Kathir sets the scene — after Allah finishes the judgement between His servants, "sending the believers to the gardens of Paradise and the disbelievers to the lows of the Fire," Iblis stands and addresses the latter. And Ibn Kathir names his motive without softening it: he speaks "in order to add depression to their depression, sorrow to their sorrow and grief to their grief."

The last thing he does for the people who followed him is deliver a speech designed to deepen their grief.

**"Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you."** Ibn Kathir: Allah's promise came "by the words of His Messengers that if you follow them, you will gain safety and deliverance" — "true and correct news." Against it stands 4:120, which Ibn Kathir cites: "He makes promises to them, and arouses in them false desires; and Shaytan's promises are nothing but deceptions."

**"I had no authority over you."** The word rendered *authority* is **سُلْطَان**, and Ibn Kathir reads it as proof rather than force: "I had no proof for what I called you to, nor evidence for what I promised you, **except that I called you, and you responded to me**." He sets this against the Messengers, who "establish the proof and unequivocal evidences against you and affirmed the truth of what they were sent to you with. But you disobeyed the Messengers and ended up earning this fate."

That is the whole indictment in a sentence. On one side: evidence, sent by Allah, established publicly. On the other: a call with nothing behind it — and a response.

**"So blame me not, but blame yourselves."** Ibn Kathir: "because it is your fault for defying the proofs and following me in the falsehood that I called you to."

**"I cannot help you, nor can you help me."** Ibn Kathir glosses both halves: "I cannot benefit, save, or deliver you from what you are suffering" — and "nor can you save me and deliver me from the torment and punishment I am suffering." The one they answered and obeyed is himself inside a punishment he wants delivering from.

**"I deny your former act of associating me as a partner with Allah."** Here the early authorities read the phrase two ways, and Ibn Kathir reports both. **Qatadah** takes it as: I disown you *because* you associated me with Allah before. **Ibn Jarir** comments: "I deny being a partner with Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored" — Shaytan repudiating the very idea that he was ever a partner.
