Ibn Kathir judges Ibn Jarir's reading "the most plausible," supporting it with 46:5–6, where those called upon besides Allah, when mankind are gathered, "will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping," and 19:82, "they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them."

The pattern in those two ayat is consistent: what was worshipped besides Allah turns against those who worshipped it.

Ibn Kathir also records a striking observation from **'Amir Ash-Sha'bi**: "On the Day of Resurrection, two speakers will address the people." The first is Allah's questioning of 'Isa, son of Maryam — "Did you say unto men: 'Worship me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'" (5:116) through to "This is a Day on which the truthful will profit from their truth" (5:119). The second is this speech of Shaytan.

The ayah closes with the verdict: **"Verily, there is a painful torment for the wrongdoers"** — whom Ibn Kathir defines as those "who deviate from truth and follow falsehood."

## Speech three: "Peace" (23)

After all that, ayah 23 arrives almost quietly. Ibn Kathir marks the turn: Allah "mentioned the final destination of the miserable ones, who earned the disgrace and torment and having to listen to Shaytan address them, then He mentioned the final destination of the happy ones."

Notice how the believers arrive: **"will be made to enter"** — they are admitted, brought in — and then **"with the permission of their Lord."** Listen to that against the rest of the passage. In ayah 21 the followers ask whether their leaders can *avail* them anything against Allah's torment, and nothing comes back. In ayah 22 Shaytan says plainly, "I cannot help you." The one entrance that opens in these three ayat opens by the permission of the Lord.

Ibn Kathir on the details: the rivers run "wherever they wish them to flow and wherever they may be" — the flow answers their wish. **خالدين فيها**, dwelling there forever: they "will never transfer or be transferred from it." They do not move on from it, and they are not moved out of it.

And the last word of the passage is the greeting: **"Their greeting therein will be: Salam."** Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels so you can hear how the Garden sounds: its gates are opened and "its keepers will say: *Salamun 'Alaykum*" (39:73); "angels shall enter unto them from every gate, saying: *Salamun 'Alaykum*" (13:23–24); "therein they shall be met with greetings and the word of peace and respect" (25:75); and their speech there runs "*Subhanaka Allahumma*... and *Salam* will be their greetings... and the close of their request will be: *Al-Hamdu Lillahi Rabbil-'Alamin*" (10:10).

Set the two vocabularies side by side. The Fire: *can you avail us anything… blame me not… blame yourselves… there is no place of refuge.* The Garden: *peace.*

## Living it

**Audit your allegiances now.** Ibn Kathir describes the followers as those who "obeyed your orders and implemented them," and their question on that Day is whether the ones they obeyed can "avail us anything against Allah's torment." That is a question worth asking early about anyone whose lead you take in your religion.

**Take Shaytan's own testimony seriously.** By his own account he had no proof and no evidence — only, in Ibn Kathir's words, "that I called you, and you responded to me." A call and a response: the ayah puts the weight on the response, which is why the next words are "blame yourselves."

**Weigh proofs, not pressure.** The Messengers, Ibn Kathir says, "establish the proof and unequivocal evidences" and "affirmed the truth of what they were sent to you with." The ruin came from defying those proofs and following a caller who had none. That is a test you can apply to what you follow today.

**Notice where the choosing happens.** "It makes no difference to us whether we rage, or bear these torments with patience" describes a place where the response you pick no longer alters the outcome. Everything in this passage that decides an outcome — following, obeying, answering a call, defying or accepting the proofs — happens before that Day arrives.

**Notice what ayah 23 names.** Those who *believed* and *did righteous deeds* — the ayah names both — and then names what brings them in: "with the permission of their Lord."

**Make salam your habit.** The Garden's greeting is peace, spoken by its keepers, by the angels at every gate, and by its people among themselves. It is worth training the tongue on that greeting now.

passages.title: Parable of the good word and evil word
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Allah sets two pictures side by side: a good word like a deep-rooted tree giving fruit in every season (ayat 24–25), and an evil word like a tree torn up from the surface of the earth, having no stability (ayah 26). Ayah 27 tells us what the first picture means in practice — that Allah Himself keeps the believer standing on that word, in this life and after death.

## Where this sits in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these ayat against ayah 18, where the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord were likened to ashes blown away by the wind on a stormy day — scattered so completely that no trace is left behind. The point there was that the deeds of disbelievers, even those that may outwardly be good, still find no acceptance with Allah. Ayah 24 then gives the similitude of the believer and his deeds, and ayah 26 that of disbelievers and hypocrites. It is the second and third panel of a single argument about what survives and what does not.

## "A good word" — what exactly?

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that **the goodly word is the testimony *lā ilāha illa-llāh*** — none has the right to be worshipped but Allah — and that **the goodly tree is the believer**. On "whose root is firmly fixed," Ibn ʿAbbās said this is *lā ilāha illa-llāh* firm in the believer's heart; and on "its branches reach to the sky," that this is that by which the believer's works ascend to heaven. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid and several others said the same, and that the parable describes the believer's deeds, his good statements and his good actions — the believer being just like the beneficial date tree, always having good actions ascending at all times.

In ayah 24 it is a goodly word likened to a goodly tree; in ayah 26 an evil word likened to an evil tree. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the correspondence: the good tree refers to the statement of the Muslim creed, *lā ilāha illa-llāh* — faith itself — and in the same manner the pairing of the bad word with the bad tree denotes the words and deeds of disbelief.

## Why a tree, and which tree

Which tree is it? The commentators differ, but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that in all likelihood it is the date palm, a view supported by experience, observation, and by ḥadīth narrations. Based on a narration of Anas, Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān and Ḥākim have reported that the Prophet ﷺ said the good tree mentioned in the Qurʼān is the date tree, and the bad tree is the *ḥanẓal* — colocynth (Mazharī).

**Al-Bukhārī** records from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that they were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he asked them to tell him about a tree that resembles the Muslim — the leaves of which do not fall in summer or winter, and which gives its fruit at all times by the leave of its Lord. Ibn ʿUmar's mind went straight to the date palm, but he felt shy to answer when he saw that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar did not speak. When they gave no answer, the Prophet ﷺ said: *It is the date palm tree.* Afterwards Ibn ʿUmar told his father, "By Allah, I thought that it was the date tree." ʿUmar asked why he had not spoken then; he said, "I saw you were silent and I felt shy to say anything." ʿUmar answered that had his son said it, it would have been more precious to him than such things. A report from Mujāhid in the *Musnad* of Aḥmad adds that someone had brought the Prophet ﷺ the pith of a date palm when he put the question.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said that the goodly tree is a tree in Paradise — the likeness reaches past anything growing in this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the date palm in particular fits the believer:

- **Its roots are deep-set and strong.** The believer's root is his faith in the *kalimah ṭayyibah*, and the accidents of the world cannot shake it out. There is no dearth of examples among the Ṣaḥābah and the Tābiʿīn, and among the staunch believers of every period, of people who cared more about their īmān and less for their life or wealth. This is *aṣluhā thābit*, "its root is firmly fixed."
- **Its fruit is out of reach of filth.** Just as a large tree remains unaffected by the impurities of the land surface, the believer keeps a concern for purity and a taste for decency, and is not affected by the pollutants of the world.
- **Its branches climb.** As the branches of the date palm are high and skyward, so are the fruits of a believer's īmān — his deeds — raised toward the heavens. It appears in the Qurʼān that good words are raised towards Allah. What a believer does in the form of remembrance of Allah, declaring His purity, saying *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, and reciting the Qurʼān keeps reaching Allah morning and evening.
- **Everything about it is of use.** Dates are eaten from the time the fruit shows up on the tree until long after it ripens, and once ripe can be stored throughout the year; even the pith is eaten, sweet juice is extracted from the trunk, mats and other articles of use are made from the leaves, and the stones make fine fodder for animals. Other trees yield fruit in particular seasons only, and not everything in them is put to some use. In the same way the believer's good deeds continue day and night, in all seasons, and his every word and deed, movement and rest, and the effects they generate, prove beneficial for the whole world — on condition, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, that he or she is a perfect believer and a faithful practitioner of the teachings of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

## "By the leave of its Lord" (ayah 25)

"Giving its fruit at all times" is said to mean by day and by night. But the ayah does not let the tree take credit for it: the fruit comes *bi-idhni rabbihā*, **by the leave of its Lord**. Ibn Kathir comments that it is thus that the fruit earns perfection and becomes beneficial, plentiful, pure and blessed. Continuity in good works is not stamina; it is permission granted.

The ayah then closes: *"and Allah sets forth parables for mankind in order that they may remember."* The likeness is given so that it will be recalled.

## The evil word (ayah 26)

Ibn Kathir says the evil word likened to an evil tree describes the disbelief of the disbeliever, for it has no basis or stability. He identifies it as similar to the colocynth tree — a very bitter, unscented plant also called *ash-Shiryān*; Shuʿbah narrated from Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Qurrah that Anas ibn Mālik said it is the colocynth tree. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that, according to others, it is garlic.

*Ujtuththat* — Ibn Kathir glosses it as "cut off from the root"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the real meaning of the word is to remove the body of something as a whole. Ibn Kathir's conclusion is that it exists without basis or stability, just like *kufr* — disbelief. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the image one step further: because the roots of that tree do not go deep into the earth, anyone can pull out the whole of it at will.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the contrast out in three matching strokes: the beliefs of a disbeliever have no root or foundation, and in no time they lose their ground; they are affected by the filth of the world around them; and the fruits of their tree — their deeds — are worthless in the sight of Allah. Ibn Kathir puts it starkly: surely, the works of the disbelievers will never ascend, nor will any of them be accepted. Which brings us back to the ashes of ayah 18.

## Ayah 27: Allah makes them firm

*Yuthabbitu-llāh* — Allah **keeps firm** those who believe, "with the word that stands firm," *al-qawl al-thābit*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān links this back to the tree: the *kalimah ṭayyibah*, the pivotal guiding principle of a believer, is a stable word — stable like a strong and firmly established tree, which is kept standing powerfully and surviving eternally by Allah, in this world and in the Hereafter as well. The tree does not hold itself up; Allah holds it up.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies that this blessed statement must be uttered with unalloyed sincerity, that its meaning must be understood fully and clearly, and that it must then be adopted as the guiding principle of life. One who believes in the *kalimah ṭayyibah* in this way is supported and strengthened by the grace of Allah, so that he stands firm by this conviction right up to the time of death, no matter how many challenges have to be encountered in its defence.

**And in the Hereafter?** Al-Bukhārī records from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: when the Muslim is questioned in the grave, he will testify that there is no deity but Allah and that Muhammad is Allah's Messenger — *hence Allah's statement,* "Allah will keep firm those who believe, with the word that stands firm in this world, and in the Hereafter." Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim and the rest of the Group recorded it too. ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded that Ṭāwūs said the firmness "in this world" is in reference to *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, and "in the Hereafter" to the questioning in the grave; Qatādah commented that as for this life, Allah will make them firm on the way of righteousness and good deeds. Ibn Kathir says several others among the Salaf said the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that it has been said in a ḥadīth of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī that "the Hereafter" in this ayah means *barzakh* — the post-death and pre-Resurrection state of life.

**What the sources describe there.** Imām Aḥmad recorded a long narration of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib (also collected by Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah): they went with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to a funeral procession of an Anṣārī man and reached the grave site when it had not yet been completed. The Prophet ﷺ sat, and they sat all around him; he held a piece of wood in his hand, poking the ground with it, then raised his head and said twice or thrice: *Seek refuge with Allah from the punishment of the grave.* He then described the believer's death — angels descending from heaven with faces white and as radiant as the sun, carrying a white shroud and fragrance from Paradise; the angel of death sitting by his head and saying, "O good and pure soul! Depart to Allah's forgiveness and pleasure"; the soul flowing out just as a drop flows out from the tip of the jug, wrapped in that shroud and fragrance, a most pleasant musk scent flowing from it, carried up through the heavens while the angels ask, "Whose is this good soul?" — until Allah says, "List my servant's record in ʿIlliyyīn and send him back to earth." The soul is joined with its body, two angels come, sit him up and ask: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? What do you say about this man who was sent to you? He answers: Allah is my Lord; my religion is Islam; he is the Messenger of Allah — and when asked what proof he has of it, he says, "I read the Book of Allah, and had faith and belief in him." A caller heralds from heaven: "My servant has said the truth." His grave is expanded for him as far as his sight can reach, a door to Paradise is opened, and a man with a handsome face, handsome clothes and pleasant scent comes to him and, asked who he is, replies, "I am your good works." The disbeliever, in the same narration, meets the mirror image — angels with dark faces, the soul seized as a thorny branch is pulled from wet wool, the gates of heaven not opened for it, his record listed in Sijjīn, and to each of the three questions only: "Oh, oh! I do not know."

The believer's reply is not something he composes under pressure; it is the word he lived on.

Imām ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd recorded in his *Musnad* from Anas ibn Mālik that when the servant is placed in his grave and his companions depart, he hears the sound of their shoes; two angels come, sit him up and ask what he says about this man, and the believer says, "I bear witness that he is Allah's servant and Messenger" — and he is told, "Look at your seat in the Fire; Allah has replaced it for you with a seat in Paradise," and he sees both. Qatādah added, "We were told that his grave will be enlarged up to seventy forearms length and will be filled with greenery for him until the Day of Judgement." Muslim collected this ḥadīth also from ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and al-Nasāʾī from Yūnus ibn Muhammad ibn al-Muʿaddah. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī recorded from Abū Hurayrah that when the dead is buried, two dark and blue angels come to him — one called Munkir and the other Nakīr — and ask what he used to say about this man; the believer bears witness, his grave is made larger for him seventy forearms by seventy and filled with light, and he is told, "Sleep, just like the bridegroom who is awakened by the dearest of his family, until Allah resurrects him." But if he was a hypocrite his answer is, "I do not know! I heard people say something, so I used to repeat what they were saying" — and the earth is commanded to come closer all around him until his ribs cross each other. Al-Tirmidhī said this ḥadīth is *ḥasan, gharīb*.

**A ḥadīth that should change how you pray tonight.** Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ swore by the One who owns his life that the dead person hears the sound of your slippers when you depart and leave him. If he is a believer, the prayer stands by his head, zakāh to his right and the fast by his left, and the righteous deeds — charity, keeping relations with kith and kin, and acts of kindness to people — stand by his feet. He is approached from his head, and the prayer declares, "No entrance from my side"; from his right, and zakāh says the same; from his left, and the fast; from his feet, and the acts of righteousness. Then he is commanded to sit up and questioned, and after his testimony his grave is made wider for him seventy forearms length and filled with light, and a door is opened for him to Paradise and he is told, "Look at what Allah has prepared for you in it," so that he only increases in joy and delight. Ibn Ḥibbān collected this ḥadīth too, his narration adding the disbeliever's answer and his torment.

**How firmly is this established?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that similar aḥādīth have been reported from about forty Ṣaḥābah with reliable chains of authorities, which Ibn Kathir has put together at this stage of his tafsīr; and that al-Suyūṭī, in his versified treatise *At-Tathbīt ʿInd at-Tabyīt* and by referring to seventy aḥādīth in *Sharḥ aṣ-Ṣudūr*, confirmed that these narrations have come down in uninterrupted (*mutawātir*) succession. That a man, after death and burial, lives again, answers the questions of the angels, and then meets reward or punishment according to success or failure in that test, is mentioned in almost ten ayat of the Qurʼān by way of hint, and very clearly in these narrations. To the doubt that nobody observes any of it, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān replies that not being able to see something is no proof of its not being present — the jinn and angels are not seen but are there, and a dreamer may writhe under a punishment in his dream while the people around him remain totally unaware. Taking one world on the analogy of the conditions prevailing in another is wrong by itself.

## "And Allah lets the wrongdoers go astray… and Allah does what He wills"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the closing of ayah 27: as for the believers, Allah keeps them firm on the *kalimah ṭayyibah* as a result of which things of comfort assemble around them right from the grave. But the unjust — the disbelievers and those who associate partners with Allah — remain deprived of this divine help; they cannot answer the questions asked in the grave by the angels Munkar and Nakīr correctly, and the outcome is that they start experiencing a sort of punishment from that point onwards.

The final clause, *"and Allah does what He wills,"* means there is no power which can block His intention and will. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from the Companions Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamānī that it is mandatory for a believer to believe that everything received by him was received through the intention and will of Allah and that not to have received it was impossible; and likewise that what was not received, it was not possible to have received — and they said that if one does not believe this and place his trust in it, his abode is Hell.

## Living it

**Fix the root before admiring the branches.** The tree's height and its fruit are consequences; *aṣluhā thābit* is the cause. So the work is on the creed itself — adopted as the guiding principle of life, which is the condition Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attaches to the whole promise.

**Aim for fruit in every season.** The date palm was chosen because it gives *at all times* — not a burst of worship in one month and bare branches the rest of the year. And "by the leave of its Lord" keeps that from becoming self-congratulation: the continuity itself is something to ask Allah for.

**Store up what will stand guard at your head.** Prayer, zakāh, fasting, charity, keeping ties of kinship, kindness to people — the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah recorded by Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī places each of them at a side of the believer in the grave. And the firm answer to "Who is your Lord?" is not produced on the spot; ayah 27 says plainly that it is Allah who keeps the believer firm. So the honest response to this passage is not confidence but a request: *O Allah, keep me firm with the word that stands firm.*

passages.title: Trading Allah's favour for disbelief and ruin
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form one accusation with one verdict. **Ayah 28** names the crime: a people took what Allah gave them as favour and put disbelief in its place — and landed their own people in "the house of destruction." **Ayah 29** names that house without ceremony: Jahannam. **Ayah 30** exposes the machinery that got them there — rivals set up beside Allah, and the pulling of others off His path — and ends with a command to the Prophet ﷺ that is at once a dismissal and a sentence: *"Say: Enjoy (your brief life)! But certainly, your destination is the (Hell) Fire!"*

What holds the three together is a single movement from a **trade** to a **destination**. Everything here is transaction and consequence.

## Where this sits in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the flow. Surah Ibrahim opens with subjects tied to the mission of the messengers and prophets, to the states of one's ultimate return, and to the Hereafter. After that comes commendation of belief in Tawhid — the Oneness of Allah — together with condemnation of disbelief and of ascribing partners to Allah, a condemnation "clarified through examples." Then those who took the second road are censured: rather than being grateful for the blessings of Allah, they chose the way of ingratitude and rejection.

Our passage is where that censure lands. In Maʿārif's words, this first verse "deplores the behaviour of disbelievers and polytheists and points out to their evil end." The verse that follows it turns to the believers — Maʿārif notes that it "describes the distinction of believers and tells them to abide by some Divine injunctions in order that they can fulfill the obligation of gratitude." Our three ayat are the warning side of that pairing.

## "Have you not seen…"

Ibn Kathir opens by quoting al-Bukhari on *alam tara*: it means **do you have knowledge of it**. It is not really a question about eyesight; it is a summons to what the listener already knows. In the same passage, other Qur'anic expressions are set beside it — *alam tara kayfa* ("Saw you not how"), *alam tara ilā alladhīna kharajū* ("Did you not think of those who went forth"), and *qawman būran*, "a lost people" (25:18).

## Who they were: Makkah, and Badr

Two early authorities are named:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas**, in a report al-Bukhari carries with a chain (ʿAli b. ʿAbdullah ← Sufyan ← ʿAmr ← ʿAta), said the ayah "is in reference to the people of Makkah."
- **ʿAli**, asked about it by Ibn al-Kawwaʾ — recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim from Abu at-Tufayl — said it refers to **the disbelievers of Quraysh on the day of Badr**.

So the passage is anchored, in these reports, to a known people and even to a named day. It is not an abstraction; it began as a verdict on identifiable men.

But Ibn Kathir does not leave the ayah locked in that moment. His text continues that this "includes all disbelievers, for Allah sent Muhammad as a mercy and a blessing to all mankind. Those who accepted this blessing and were thankful for it, will enter Paradise, while those who denied it and disbelieved in it, will enter the Fire." A verdict on a particular people — and a standing principle for everyone the message ever reaches.

## What exactly was traded away

The passage turns on the word **niʿmah**, "favour" or "blessing." Two complementary readings are given.

**In Ibn Kathir's text:** "the blessing of Allah was faith that came to the polytheists of Quraysh, and they changed this blessing into disbelief and led their people to utter destruction." On this reading the gift they threw away was faith itself — and the disbelief consisted, as the passage puts it elsewhere, in denying Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his message.

**In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:** *niʿmat Allah* here can carry two whole classes of gift. First the **physical** blessings — "tangible and perceptible," relating to outward benefit: food, drink, land, home and things like that. Second the **spiritual** blessings sent for humanity's guidance: the prophets, the scriptures, and "the signs of Divine power and wisdom which have been placed in every inch of the human existence, and in its countless creations, and in the heavens and its unfathomable and incomprehensible universe." Maʿārif calls all of this "logistics for the guidance of human beings" — everything needed for the journey, put in place beforehand.

Both classes of gift made one and the same demand: that human beings "should have recognized the greatness and the power of Allah Taʿala, been grateful to His gifts and devoted to His command." Recognition, then gratitude, then obedience. "But, the disbelievers and the polytheists elected to shun gratitude and obedience and opted for ingratitude and disobedience."

**A word on the verb.** Ayah 28 does not say they *lost* the favour or *neglected* it. *Baddalū* — they **changed it for**, put something else in its place. Disbelief here is not simply the absence of faith; it is what they handed back over the counter in exchange for what they had been given. Maʿārif, describing the same choice, calls it "a strange exchange indeed."

## "…and caused their people to dwell in the house of destruction"

The second half of ayah 28 stacks a second crime on the first. *Aḥallū qawmahum* — they lodged, settled, **landed** their own people in *dār al-bawār*, the house of destruction. A man may destroy himself; these men took their people down with them. Maʿārif: "they led their people to their mutual abode of destruction, that is, in Hell."

## Ayah 29: the name, and the abode

Ayah 28 speaks by description — "the house of destruction." Ayah 29 supplies the name: **Jahannam**. *Yaṣlawnahā* — in it they will burn. Maʿārif renders it simply: "They shall enter it."

Then the closing phrase: *wa biʾsa al-qarār* — "what an evil place for settlement," or in Maʿārif's rendering, "an evil abode." Note what the passage does here. Maʿārif listed *home* among the physical blessings these people had been given; and the place they end up is described in exactly those terms — not a stop along the way, but an abode, somewhere to settle. The gift and the punishment are named with the same kind of word.

## Ayah 30: rivals — and the pulling of others

*Andād* is the plural of **nidd**, which Maʿārif defines as "like and equal." Idols are called *andād*, it explains, because the disbelievers, **through their deeds**, used to regard them as the like or equal of Allah.

That phrase — through their deeds — is worth carrying away. Maʿārif locates the equating in what people did. Ibn Kathir describes the same thing in terms of action: "they set up partners to Allah whom they worship besides Him and called the people to worship them."

And then *li-yuḍillū ʿan sabīlih* — "to mislead from His path." Their error was not kept to themselves; on Ibn Kathir's reading they called others to it. This is the same outward motion as ayah 28, where they did not merely fall into destruction but *landed their people* there. Misguidance in this passage always travels.

## "Say: Enjoy!"

Ibn Kathir notes that "Allah threatened them and warned them by the words of His Prophet ﷺ" — the imperative *qul*, "Say," puts the warning in the Prophet's ﷺ own mouth.

*Tamattaʿū* is imperative in form but it is not permission. Maʿārif glosses *tamattuʿ* as "the driving of temporary benefit out of something" — squeezing short-term use from a thing that will not last; and it reads the verse as telling them to enjoy the blessings of the mortal world for a while, since their ultimate abode is the fire of Hell. Ibn Kathir paraphrases the sense the same way: "Whatever you are able to do in this life, then do it, for no matter what will happen … to Us will be your destination and end."

Now set the passage's two key nouns side by side and the whole argument stands complete in miniature:

- **tamattuʿ** (ayah 30) — temporary benefit, briefly extracted;
- **qarār** (ayah 29) — the abode they settle in.

They chose the first, and with it purchased the second.

Ibn Kathir brings two other ayat that state the identical pattern: *"We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall force them to (enter) a great torment"* (31:24), and *"(A brief) enjoyment in this world! And then unto Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they used to disbelieve"* (10:70). In each, the enjoyment is real and short; and in each, what is punished is the disbelief.

## The lesson these ayat carry

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the passage's teaching out explicitly. What these verses display is "the greatness, virtues, blissfulness and fruitfulness of the belief in the Oneness of Allah and in the Kalimah Taiyyibah: *la ilaha illallah*," and, held up against it, "the ill effect and evil outcome of refusing to believe in them."

Tawhid, it says, "is an everlasting treasure which is full of barakah in many ways. In the present world of our experience, it brings Divine support with it, and which continues after that too, in the ʾAkhirah and the grave."

And then the sharpest line of the commentary: rejecting it "amounts to changing what was the blessing and favour of Allah into what is punishment."

Read that carefully. On this reading the punishment is not some separate thing bolted onto the blessing afterwards. It is the blessing itself, **turned**. Food, drink, land, a home, the prophets, the scriptures — every item on Maʿārif's list is a gift that can be received with gratitude or handed back as denial, and the same item answers for the one who chose.

## Living it

This is a passage about disbelief, and it should not be stretched into a lash for every ordinary shortcoming. But two things fall out of it plainly.

**Gratitude is a response, not a mood.** Maʿārif frames *niʿmah* as something that makes a demand: the blessings "demanded that human beings should have recognized the greatness and the power of Allah Taʿala, been grateful to His gifts and devoted to His command." Recognition, gratitude, obedience — a sequence that ends in action.

**Look at the deeds.** Since Maʿārif locates the equating of idols with Allah in what people did — "through their deeds" — the honest question is behavioural: what am I actually treating as though it stood level with Allah, in what I fear, in what I chase, in what I will not give up?

And the passage does not end on the warning. The very next verse, Maʿārif notes, turns to the believers and tells them how to "fulfill the obligation of gratitude" — which is to say that the alternative to this bad trade is not merely avoiding it, but a life that takes what Allah gives and answers with obedience.

passages.title: Prayer, gratitude, and Allah's uncountable favours
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about**

Allah commands that His believing servants be told two things — establish the prayer and spend from the sustenance He has given them — and attaches a deadline to both: do it *before* a Day arrives on which there is neither mutual bargaining nor befriending (ayah 31). The three ayat that follow (32–34) supply the reason: a sweeping inventory of the favours by which Allah sustains us — the heavens and earth, rain and fruit, ships and rivers, sun and moon, night and day — closing with the admission that these favours cannot be counted, and the blunt verdict that the human being is nevertheless "an extreme wrongdoer, ungrateful."

The passage moves from **what is owed** (ayah 31), to **why it is owed** (32–33), to **how poorly we usually pay it** (34).

## Ayah 31: two commands and a closing window

Ibn Kathir reads the two commands as covering both halves of religious life: "Allah orders His servants to obey Him, fulfil His rights and be kind to His creatures." Prayer is the right of Allah — it "affirms the worship of Allah alone, without partners." Spending is kindness to His creation — and Ibn Kathir spells out its breadth: paying the due Zakah, spending on relatives, and being kind to all others.

**What establishing the prayer involves.** Ibn Kathir gives the list without abbreviation: establishing the prayer requires performing it *on time*, performing it *perfectly*, preserving its act of bowing, having humility during it, and preserving its prostrations.

**Secretly and openly.** The ayah specifies that the spending be done both in private and in public, and Ibn Kathir gives the purpose simply: "so that the people save themselves."

**Now is the time to act.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on the urgency in "before there comes a day." Allah has blessed you, right now, with the necessary strength and time to make your prayer; and if prayers have been missed in the past through negligence, this is the window in which to make amends and do the *qaḍāʾ* — the replacement of missed prayers. Your wealth, likewise, is in your possession *today*, and by spending it in the way of Allah you can make it work for you, particularly for the good of your eternal life. The day is coming when both these options will be taken away: bodies will no longer remain active enough for prayer, and no wealth will remain in your possession with which to pay for rights wasted.

## "No trade and no friendship" — what the Day removes

**Trade (*bayʿ*).** Ibn Kathir explains that on that Day "no ransom will be accepted from anyone, if he seeks to buy himself," and cites Allah's words elsewhere: *So this Day no ransom shall be taken from you, nor of those who disbelieved* (57:15). He then states his own conclusion plainly — no mutual bargaining or ransom will avail anyone that Day, "even if he ransoms himself with the earth's fill of gold if he could find that amount." Maʿārif adds the practical point: on that day there will be no buying and selling, no transactions through which one could buy something, through which one could expiate for shortcomings and sins.

**Friendship (*khilāl*).** Here the meaning turns on the Arabic, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings of *khilāl*. It can be taken as the plural form of *khullah*, which means selfless friendship. Or it can be taken as a verbal noun of the derived form the grammarians call *mufāʿalah* — Maʿārif's examples of that form are *qitāl* and *difāʿ* — in which case it would mean a friendship between two persons which is mutual and sincere.

Ibn Jarir, quoted by Ibn Kathir, states what this cancels: "on that Day, there will be no friendship between friends that might save those deserving punishment from it. Rather, on that Day, there will be fairness and justice." Maʿārif puts it at the human scale: no friend, no matter how dear, will be able to carry the burden of sins committed by another, nor will he find any way to somehow remove the punishment due against him.

Maʿārif also observes that this closing sentence relates to **both** injunctions, the prayer and the charity alike — the deadline covers the whole verse, not just the giving.

**Which Day?** Maʿārif notes that *yawm* here obviously means the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Judgement. But it adds a second, unsettling possibility: it could also be said that it may be the day of one's death, because all these signs start showing up immediately from the time of death — one is left without any ability to do anything, nor does wealth stay in the possession of its owner as he leaves the world behind. On that reading, the deadline is not distant at all.

## Which friendships survive

Qatadah's comment, preserved by Ibn Kathir, turns the warning into a criterion for choosing company: "Allah knows that in this life, there is mutual bargaining and there are friendships which people benefit from. A man chooses his friends and the reasons behind befriending them; if it was for Allah's sake, their friendship should be maintained, but if it was for other than Allah, their friendship is bound to be cut off."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same distinction and states the qualification precisely: what will not work on the Day of Judgement are friendships **based solely on material interests**. Those who maintain friendships and relationships for the sake of Allah, and for what is done to serve the interests of His revealed religion, will still work at that time as well — because the good servants of Allah who are accepted in His sight will intercede on behalf of others, as has been reported in many ahadith. The Qurʼān itself makes the exception: those who were friends to each other in the life of the world will turn into enemies to one another, each wishing to put the blame for his sin on a friend and absolve himself of it, **"except those who fear Allah"** (43:67). The people of taqwā — those who act right in fear of Allah — will be able to put in a good word for each other by way of helping them out.

Ibn Kathir closes the point with a boundary that must not be blurred: no friendship and no intercession shall avail a person "if he meets Allah while a disbeliever" — quoting *And fear the Day when no person shall avail another, nor shall compensation be accepted from him, nor shall intercession be of use to him, nor shall they be helped* (2:123), and the parallel command in 2:254.

## Ayat 32–33: the inventory of favours

Having issued the command, Allah now recounts the grounds for it. Maʿārif frames these ayat as a recounting of Allah's major blessings by which human beings are invited to worship and obey Him — the argument being that it is Allah alone who created the heavens and the earth, on which the emergence and survival of human existence depend.

Ibn Kathir walks through the list: Allah created **the heavens as a protective ceiling and the earth as a bed**; He sends down **rain** from the sky and, in its aftermath, brings forth a variety of vegetation, fruits and plants "of different colors, shapes, tastes, scents and uses" — the variety itself being part of the gift. He made **ships** sail on the surface of the water by His command, and made the sea able to carry them, so travellers can transfer from one area to another and goods be transported. He created **rivers** flowing through the earth from one area to another as provision for the servants, which they use to drink and irrigate, and for other benefits besides.

**The word *thamarāt*.** Maʿārif points out that *ath-thamarāt* is the plural of *thamarah*, which is the end product of everything — not just what hangs on a tree. So everything that becomes for human beings their food, dress or a home to live in is included under it, since the word *rizq* ("sustenance") in this ayah covers all human needs (Mazhari).

## *Sakhkhara* — the key word of the passage

Repeatedly the passage says Allah *subjected* things to you — the ships, the rivers, the sun and the moon, the night and the day. What this verb does and does not mean is the interpretive heart of these two ayat.

**With the ships: subjection means He made their use easy for you.** That is Maʿārif's gloss on *sakhkhara* — that Allah has made the use of these things easy on you. Of course there is wood and steel and the instrumentation and technology to build boats and ships; but when it comes to having the intelligence and the ability to use them correctly and expertly, it must be admitted that these were all given by Him. Maʿārif turns this on the inventor's pride: how can someone who works with wood, iron and copper, uses them to serve his end product, and then goes about declaring himself its inventor? Not one of the things he used was created by him, nor could he have created them. And, Maʿārif adds, "this very existence of ours, our hands and feet, our mind and our intelligence are not what we have made or invented."

**With the sun and the moon, subjection emphatically does not mean they move at your command.** Maʿārif imagines the alternative with some wit: had the sun and the moon been subjugated in a way that they moved under human command, there would have been mutual differences among people over them — one demanding that the sun rise two hours later than usual because he had too much work to do in the night, another wanting it two hours earlier because he had too many daytime jobs at hand. So the great Lord did, in a way, subjugate the sun and the moon for human beings, but in the sense that they have been subjugated to serve human beings all the time and under all conditions under a wise Divine arrangement — not that their rising and setting and their speed become subservient to human pleasure. The same holds for the night and the day: both have been put in the service of human beings to provide convenience and comfort.

**"*Dāʾibayn*" — the two that never break their habit.** Maʿārif traces this word to *daʾb*, which means habit. The sense is that moving at all times and under all conditions has been made the habit of these two, as it never happens contrary to that. Ibn Kathir describes them as rotating by night and by day, and gathers the parallel verses: *It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day. They all float, each in an orbit* (36:40); and *(He created) the sun, the moon, the stars subjected to His command. His is the creation and commandment* (7:54). The night and the day are opposites, he notes, each taking from the length of the other or giving up some of its own — *(Allah) merges the night into day, and merges the day into night* (35:13) — and each of the two runs "on a fixed course for an appointed term" (39:5).

## Ayah 34: given more than you asked for

**"And He gave you of all that you asked for."** Ibn Kathir reads this as: He has prepared for you all that you need in all conditions, and what you ask Him to provide for you.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further: what Allah is pleased to give does not depend on being asked by someone for it. *We had never asked for our existence itself.* Who had raised hands of prayer that the skies, the earth, the moon, the sun and so many other things be created for us? The Master simply gave all this, without our asking. For this reason al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī explained the phrase as: **"Allah has given you everything which is worth asking for, even if you have not actually asked for it."**

**What about prayers that seem unanswered?** Maʿārif answers directly. Even if the meaning intended is what the words literally suggest, it poses no problem — for what a person generally asks for is usually given to him anyway. And wherever what he asks for is not given in the outward form it was sought, there is in that some expedient consideration, for the person asking or for the rest of the world, which he does not know about. He who is All-Knowing and All-Aware knows that, were that request to be granted, it would become for him, or for his family, or for the whole world, a curse. In such a case, **not giving what has been asked for becomes, in itself, a great blessing.** But because he lacks that knowledge, the human being cannot realise it, and so he feels disappointed.

## "If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you could never count them"

Ibn Kathir states the plain sense: the servants are never able to count Allah's blessings, let alone thank Him duly for them.

Maʿārif expands it until the mind gives up trying. Even if all human beings combined together were to count them, they would still remain uncountable. A human being is, as is, a little world: in the eyes, the nose, the ears, the hands, the feet, in every joint — rather, in every muscle and vein — endless blessings lie hidden, through which this wonderful walking, pulsating creature keeps busy doing all sorts of things through hundreds of very delicate mechanisms. Then there is the mind-boggling range of Divine creation, above the earth, on it and beneath it, in the seas and the mountains — much of which, despite the revealing research done in modern times and the devotion of thousands of experts who have spent their lives at the work, still remains undocumented or unidentified.

And then Maʿārif corrects our very definition of a blessing. We tend to take as blessings only what comes in a positive and perceptible way. In fact, blessings are not restricted by that definition: **remaining safe from diseases, hardships, pain, loss and sorrows is a standing blessing in its own right** — and a person could hardly be expected to keep a count of all the afflictions of body and soul he has been spared.

**From the Sunnah.** It is recorded in Sahih Al-Bukhari that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to supplicate: *"O Allah! All praise is due to You, without being able to sufficiently thank You, nor ever wish to be cut off from You, nor ever feeling rich from relying on You; our Lord!"* Gratitude here is offered together with the confession that it falls short — that is the model.

Ibn Kathir also reports that the Prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, used to say in his supplication: "O Lord! How can I ever duly thank You, when my thanking You is also a favour from You to me?" And Allah the Exalted answered him: "Now, you have thanked Me sufficiently, O Dawud" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, *when you admitted that you will never be able to duly thank Me.*

Maʿārif draws out the mercy in this. Justice demanded that, in return for these countless blessings, equally countless acts of obedience and equally countless demonstrations of gratitude should have been made mandatory. But Allah, in His infinite grace, showed leniency towards intrinsic human weakness: when a person looks at reality and confesses that fulfilling the demands of obligatory gratitude is not within his control, **that very confession has been declared sufficient as the alternative to the ideal fulfilment of the obligation** — as it was in the answer given to Sayyidnā Dawud, peace be upon him.

## "Indeed, mankind is truly unjust, entirely ungrateful"

The ayah ends on *ẓalūm kaffār*, rendered by Maʿārif as "very unjust, very ungrateful."

Maʿārif defines the standard the human being fails to meet. He should face hardship with patience, keeping his words and feelings free from any complaint, thinking that the fate he faces has come from a wise Master and that this, being from His infinite Wisdom, is nothing but a blessing. And when he is blessed with what is good and comforting, let him be thankful for it from his heart, both verbally and practically — as is the dictate of justice.

Common human habit works differently from this norm. A little discomfort or pain and people lose patience and go about broadcasting their problem. And if they find some blessing or a little wealth, they get intoxicated with it and forget all about Allah, their Benefactor.

This is why, as Maʿārif points out, a verse appearing earlier in the same sūrah — ayah 5 — identifies the attribute of sincere believers as *ṣabbār* (very patient) and *shakūr* (very grateful).

## Living it

- **Guard the prayer as Ibn Kathir describes it** — on time, performed perfectly, its bowing preserved, humility within it, its prostrations preserved.
- **Make up what was missed.** Maʿārif's advice is direct: if prayers were lost through negligence, do their qaḍāʾ now, while you still have the strength and the time.
- **Give in both registers**, secretly and openly: the Zakah that is due, then relatives, then kindness to all others.
- **Audit your friendships** by Qatadah's test: is this bond for Allah's sake, or for other than Allah?
- **Reread an unanswered duʿāʾ** as possible protection you cannot yet see, rather than as neglect.
- **Count what you were spared**, not only what you were given — safety from disease, hardship, pain, loss and sorrow is itself a standing blessing.
- **When you cannot thank enough, say so.** Maʿārif teaches that this confession has itself been accepted in place of the gratitude we could never fully discharge.

passages.title: Abraham's prayer for Makkah and his offspring
passages.tafsir:
**These seven ayat are one long supplication.** Ibrahim (peace be upon him) stands before his Lord and asks — for a city, for his children, for the prayer, and finally for forgiveness. Simply a prophet praying, with the Qur'an letting us listen.

## Why this prayer, and why here

Earlier in the surah (ayah 28) Allah condemned "those who changed the favour of Allah with disbelief" — the disbelievers of Makkah, who had traded faith for denial and the Oneness of Allah for shirk because that was what their forefathers did. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Al-Bahr Al-Muhit) explains that the story of Ibrahim is placed here as the answer to exactly that argument: you want to follow your ancestors — then look at your real patriarch.

Ibn Kathir puts the same point sharply. Allah is bringing evidence against the Arab polytheists that the Sacred House in Makkah was founded on the worship of Allah alone, without partners — and that the very man who established the city disowned those who worship anything besides Allah.

As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, when the Qur'an tells the stories of the prophets it never aims at history alone; these episodes carry guiding principles for every department of human life.

## The moment behind ayah 37

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells the story behind ayah 37: Allah willed that the Baytullah — destroyed in the Deluge of Nuh's time — be rebuilt, and chose His *khalīl* ("friend," or as Ibn Kathir renders it, Allah's intimate friend), Ibrahim, for the task, arranging for him to migrate from Syria with his wife Hajira and his son Ismaʿil and settle in that barren place.

It appears in the Sahih of Al-Bukhari that Ismaʿil was an infant at the time. Ibrahim, as ordered, left him and his mother near the site of the present Baytullah and the well of Zamzam — open, barren ground ringed by hills, no water, no habitation in sight. He had put some food in a provision-bag and water in a water-bag.

Then came the command to return to Syria — and he obeyed on the spot. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on this: he would not tolerate the least delay, not even the few moments it would have taken to go to his wife, explain that this was a divine order, and say a word of comfort. Hajira called after him again and again — why would he leave them like this, with no human being around and nothing to help them survive? The friend of Allah did not look back. Then it dawned on her that a man who is Allah's friend could not betray them so; perhaps this was a command from Allah. So she called again: "Has Allah commanded you to leave this place?" He turned his face and said: "Yes." And she said: *idhan lā yuḍayyiʿunā* — "Now it does not matter. Our Master, who commanded you to leave this place, will certainly not let us be wasted away."

He kept walking until he reached a hill from which he could no longer see them. There he turned toward the Baytullah and prayed the words of ayah 37.

**Two things at once.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this shows. On one side, he discharged his obligation as the friend of Allah: the command came, and he moved, without the least hesitation. On the other, he did not neglect what his family had a right to from him — praying, once they were out of sight, that they be protected and blessed with peace. He could ask with confidence, knowing that a prayer made after carrying out the divine command would never be rejected by the merciful Lord. And so it happened: the helpless infant and his equally helpless mother found shelter, a whole city flowered around them and for their sake, and the doors of every kind of blessing remain open to the people of Makkah to this day.

This, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is prophetic steadfastness and the beauty of balance. Prophets are not like common mystics overpowered by the state they are in (*maghlūb al-ḥāl*); prophets educate, and it is their education that makes a human being complete.

## Two prayers, two different days

Ayah 35 and ayah 37 were not said on the same occasion, and the Arabic itself shows it.

In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:126) Ibrahim says *rabbi ijʿal hādhā **baladan** āminan* — "a city," indefinite, with no *alif-lām*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this prayer belonged to a time when Makkah was not yet inhabited, so the wording had to be general. Here in ayah 35 he says *hādhā **al-balad*** — "this city," definite — because by then Makkah was already a populated city.

Ibn Kathir reads the sequence the same way. Ibrahim says "this city" after he had established it, and that is why ayah 39 follows with "All praise is due to Allah, Who has given me in old age Ismaʿil and Ishaq" — and it is well known that Ismaʿil was thirteen years older than Ishaq. When Ibrahim took Ismaʿil and his mother to Makkah the child was still young enough to nurse, and that was the occasion of 2:126.

An editor's note in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties it off: ayah 37 belongs to the day he left them in the valley; ayah 35 came at a later stage. There is no contradiction.

**And Allah accepted it.** Ibn Kathir cites the answer from elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Have they not seen that We have made (Makkah) a secure sanctuary" (29:67), and "the first House appointed for mankind was that at Bakkah… whosoever enters it attains security" (3:96–97).

## "Keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols"

Prophets are protected by Allah — shirk, idol-worship and sin cannot issue from them. So why does Ibrahim include *himself*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons: either because the prophets too live under a constant fear of being in danger, or because his main purpose was his children, and he included himself to impress on them how grave the matter is.

Ibn Kathir draws a rule of etiquette from the same words: whoever supplicates should ask for the benefit of his parents and his offspring along with himself.

**A hard question.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that Allah granted the prayer of His friend, and his children remained protected from shirk and idol-worship. But the people of Makkah are generally from among Ibrahim's progeny, and idol-worship was very much present among them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, on the authority of Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah: no one from the progeny of Ismaʿil really took to idol-worship. When the tribe of Jurhum took over Makkah and expelled Ismaʿil's children from the Haram, they carried away some stones from there out of love and respect for the sacred place, and kept them as a memento of the House of Allah — placing them before themselves when they worshipped, and making tawaf around them. Initially they had no desire to turn away from Allah; they thought that since praying towards the Baytullah and circling it is nothing but worship of Allah, turning to a stone taken from there and circling it would not be counter to that. After a passage of time, this very method became the cause of idol-worship.

**Idols in the wider sense.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some noble mystics of Islam read "idols" here more broadly: everything which makes a person heedless of Allah is his idol, and when, overcome by love of it, he disobeys Allah, that is in a way its worship. On that reading, asking to be kept from idol-worship covers being kept from all sins. As Rumi said: "Every (evil) desire is an idol in your way."

## "Whoever disobeys me — then You are Forgiving, Merciful" (ayah 36)

In ayah 36 Ibrahim gives his reason: the idols "have led astray many among mankind." He had seen his own father and his people fall victim to that custom, which had left them deprived of all possibilities of betterment.

Then the delicate close: "whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me — then You are Most Forgiving, Very Merciful." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works through it. If "disobeys" means evil deeds, such people too could hope to be forgiven by His good grace. But if it means disbelief, denial and rejection, Ibrahim had already been told there is no forgiveness for the disbeliever and the one who ascribes partners to Allah, and that he should not intercede for them — so expressing a hope of their forgiveness cannot be correct.

Al-Bahr Al-Muhit resolves it: at this place Ibrahim used no words that would suggest a recommendation or a prayer. He did not say "forgive them." Nevertheless he was a prophet of abounding mercy, and every prophet wishes from the deep recesses of his heart that no one should ever be subjected to divine punishment, not even a disbeliever.

Ibn Kathir observes that ʿIsa (peace be upon him) said something closely parallel: "If You punish them, they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, verily You, only You, are the Almighty, the All-Wise" (5:118) — a supplication that refers this and all matters back to Allah, not a statement that it is actually going to happen. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as: if You were to forgive them, then You have the Might and the Wisdom; there is no one to stop You. Both of these blessed souls kept within the etiquette due before Allah: neither took the initiative of recommending forgiveness for disbelievers, and neither asked that they be punished.

**The Prophet ﷺ and these two verses.** Ibn Kathir records that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Ibrahim's words, "O my Lord! They have indeed led astray many among mankind," and ʿIsa's words, "If You punish them, they are Your servants," then raised his hands and said, "O Allah, save my Ummah! O Allah, save my Ummah! O Allah, save my Ummah!" — and cried. Allah said to the angel Jibril, "Go to Muhammad — and your Lord has more knowledge — and ask him what makes him cry." Jibril came and asked, and the Prophet ﷺ repeated to him what he had said. Allah said, "Go to Muhammad and tell him: We will make you pleased with your Ummah, O Muhammad, and will not treat them in a way you dislike."

## Inside the words of ayah 37

**"A valley of no vegetation" (*ghayri dhī zarʿ*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices what Ibrahim did *not* say. He did not say "a valley with no water," because from the command itself he had become certain that Allah would not let them perish and would somehow provide them with water. He said: no vegetation. So he asked instead that they be blessed with *fruits* — even if they had to be brought in from somewhere else. That is why Makkah al-Mukarramah has no significant areas of cultivation to this day, yet fruits and produce of all sorts reach there from all over the world in numbers and variety hard to match in many cities (Al-Bahr Al-Muhit). Ibn Kathir cites the acceptance: "Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which are brought fruits of all kinds, a provision from Ourselves" (28:57).

**"Fruits" (*thamarāt*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *thamrah* customarily means fruit that is eaten, but it also carries the sense of outcome and produce — the *thamrah* of an industry is its product, of a job the pay received for it. In 28:57 Allah says "fruits of every *thing*" (*shayʾ*), not "of every *tree*" (*shajar*) — perhaps indicating that Ibrahim prayed not merely for fruits to eat but for the end product of everything beneficial.

**"By Your Sacred House" (*ʿinda baytika al-muḥarram*).** The phrase proves the foundation of the House had been laid before Ibrahim's time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from Al-Qurtubi that Adam (peace be upon him) first raised the structure when he was sent to the earth, Jibril directing him to the site; he and his children performed tawaf around it until the Deluge of Nuh's time, when the sacred House was raised up and only its foundations remained embedded under the earth. Ibrahim was commanded to build anew on those existing foundations, which Jibril identified and showed to him. When the Abrahamic structure later collapsed in the age of Arab Jahiliyyah the Quraysh rebuilt it — and Abu Talib, along with the Prophet ﷺ before he was made a prophet, took part in that work.

*Muḥarram* means "sanctified," and can also mean "protected." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the great Baytullah has both attributes: always sanctified and esteemed, and always protected from enemies.

**"That they may establish the prayer."** Ibn Jarir At-Tabari, quoted by Ibn Kathir, connects this back to *al-muḥarram*: You made this House sacred so that people would establish the prayer next to it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses the order: this was the first thing Ibrahim asked for, right after mentioning the helplessness of his infant son and his mother — that they be made punctual in *salah*, because salah is a cumulative receptacle of everything good and blissful in life, mortal or eternal.

And notice the grammar: he had left behind only one mother and one child, yet the prayer he made was in the **plural** ("that *they* may establish the prayer"). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān infers that Ibrahim had come to know that this place would have a populated city of its own and that this child's line would flourish and go far in time — so he included all of them in his prayer.

**"Hearts among men" (*afʾidatan mina al-nās*).** *Afʾidah* is the plural of *fuʾād*, heart. Here it is indefinite and paired with *min*, the particle used for reducing, dividing and portioning — "hearts of a number of the people." Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Saʿid bin Jubayr that had he said "the hearts of mankind," Persians, Romans, Jews, Christians and all other people would have gathered around it; by saying "among men" he made it exclusive to the Muslims.

## The closing sequence: ayat 38–41

**Ayah 38 — "You know what we conceal and what we reveal."** Ibn Kathir, quoting Ibn Jarir At-Tabari, gives the sense: *You know the intention behind my supplication for the people of this town — that I seek Your pleasure in sincerity to You.* And, as the same passage continues, You know all things, apparent and hidden, and nothing escapes Your knowledge on the earth or in heaven.

**Ayah 39 — praise before more asking.** He breaks off from requests to praise and thank his Lord for granting him offspring after he became old: "All praise is due to Allah, Who has given me in old age Ismaʿil and Ishaq." Ibn Kathir explains the closing words — "my Lord is indeed the All-Hearer of invocations" — as Ibrahim testifying from experience: He accepts the supplication of those who invoke Him, and He accepted my invocation when I asked Him to grant me offspring. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this a method: earnest pleading and humble plaint alongside the recounting of Allah's praises is the manner in which a prayer can be strongly hoped to be answered.

**Ayah 40 — "Make me one who establishes the prayer."** Ibn Kathir glosses *muqīm al-salāh* as one who preserves its obligations and its limits — not merely performing it, but keeping it whole. He asks that his offspring be made among those who establish the prayer as well, and then: "our Lord, and accept my invocation" — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, all of the invocation he made here.

**Ayah 41 — the last request is forgiveness.** "Our Lord! Forgive me and my parents, and the believers on the Day when the reckoning will be established." Ibn Kathir notes that Ibrahim said this before he declared himself innocent of his father, which came after he became sure that his father was an enemy of Allah. "The believers" means all of them; and the Day the reckoning is established is the Day Allah will reckon His servants and recompense them for their deeds — good for good and evil for evil.

## What the passage asks of us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames it plainly: as for *duʿāʾ* — supplication, calling on Allah — everyone makes it, but not everyone knows how. The prayers of the blessed prophets teach us how to ask, and what is worth asking for.

- **Ask for security first.** If people remain insecure where they live, their lives can never be pleasant, materially or spiritually — and even in religious terms, one can obey the divine commands only when one has the necessary peace to do so. Through that one sentence in ayah 35, Ibrahim asked for his children everything that matters in this world.
- **Provide for your family — this is not the opposite of detachment.** From that same first prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws that emotional concern for one's children, and the arrangement of economic sufficiency for them, is one of the obligations placed on the father, to the best of his ability; making efforts for this is not contrary to *zuhd* (having no greed for worldly pleasures).
- **Then ask for what security is for.** Shirk and idol-worship are sins for which there is no forgiveness, so he asked to be shielded against them; a sin committed after that can be expiated through other deeds, and such sins could also be forgiven through someone's intercession.
- **Put the prayer at the top of what you want for your children** — as he did for a family left in a valley with no vegetation and no neighbours.
- **Obey first, then ask.** He carried out the command before he raised his hands.
- **Include others.** He prayed for himself, his parents, his offspring, and the believers, all of them, on the Day when the reckoning will be established.

passages.title: Allah is never unaware of wrongdoers' deeds
passages.tafsir:
**What these ayat are doing**

This passage speaks to the unease of anyone who watches wrongdoing prosper and sees nothing happen to the wrongdoer. Its answer is that nothing is being missed: a Day has been fixed, and a full account is being kept until then.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Sūrah Ibrāhīm has mentioned matters relating to the prophets and their peoples, the evil end of those who opposed the divine injunctions, and then Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) himself — who constructed the Baytullah (the House of Allah), and for whose children Allah made a community rise around them in Makkah al-Mukarramah, providing all its inhabitants perfect peace and extraordinary economic facilities. Those children, the Banū Ismāʿīl (the descendants of Ismāʿīl), are the first addressees of the Glorious Qur'an and of the Prophet ﷺ. In this last section of the sūrah, says Maʿārif, those same people of Makkah are exhorted to take a lesson from what happened to past peoples, and warned that if they still do not return to their senses, they had better be ready to face the horrendous punishment of the Day of Qiyāmah — the Day of Resurrection.

The five ayat move as a single unit. Ayah 42 says the delay is not inattention. Ayah 43 shows the Day the account falls due. Ayah 44 puts a plea in the wrongdoers' mouths and lets Allah answer it with their own old oaths. Ayah 45 asks why the ruins they live among taught them nothing. Ayah 46 closes the file on their scheming.

## Ayah 42: the delay is not neglect

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Muhammad, do not think that Allah is unaware of what the unjust disbelievers do." And he immediately names the mistake being ruled out — *do not think that because Allah gave them respite and delayed their punishment, He is unaware, or is ignoring punishing them for what they do.* Rather, Ibn Kathir says, "Allah keeps full account of this for them and keeps it on record against them."

That is the theology of the whole passage in one line. Respite — that Allah *defers* them, يُؤَخِّرُهُمْ — is not amnesty. Nothing is slipping past Allah; a record is being kept.

**Who is being addressed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the question directly. On the words "And never think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers are doing," it says the address is obviously to every such person whom his own negligence, and shayṭān (the devil), have tricked into believing something like that. And should it be that the Prophet ﷺ himself is the addressee here, still the purpose of saying it would be to let the negligent of the community hear it and be warned — "because, there exists just no possibility that the Holy Prophet ﷺ would … ever think that Allah Taʿālā is unaware or indifferent to what is happening."

**Two audiences, one verse.** Maʿārif notes that ayah 42 does two things at once. Initially it is to comfort the Prophet ﷺ and the oppressed of the world. Then it releases the threat of a severe punishment for all oppressors: the unjust practitioners of crime should not become carefree because Allah Taʿālā has given them respite. Let them not be deluded by the idea that Allah is not aware of their wrongdoings, for which reason they are flourishing despite their crimes and nothing unwelcome happens to them. This is not true. Everything they are doing is within the sight of Allah Taʿālā — but He, "in His mercy and wisdom, is giving them respite."

Hold both halves together. To the wronged, the ayah says: you have not been forgotten. To the wrongdoer it says: the quiet you are enjoying is not a verdict of innocence.

## Ayat 42–43: the Day the eyes will not blink

The rest of ayah 42 fixes the deadline — "a Day when the eyes will stare in horror" — which Ibn Kathir explains as being "from the horror of the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir then says Allah mentions how they will all be raised up from their graves and hurriedly gathered for the Day of Gathering. Ayah 43 films that scene in four quick strokes.

**مُهْطِعِينَ (*muhṭiʿīn*) — "hastening forward."** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: in a hurry. He gathers other ayat that show the same rushing: "Hastening towards the caller" (54:8); "On that Day mankind will follow strictly Allah's caller, no crookedness will they show him" (20:108) — through to "And (all) faces shall be humbled before the Ever Living, the Sustainer" (20:111); and "The Day when they will come out of the graves quickly" (70:43).

**مُقْنِعِي رُءُوسِهِمْ (*muqniʿī ruʾūsihim*) — "with necks outstretched."** Ibn Kathir explains this as raising their heads up, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and several others — the heads raised towards the sky. Maʿārif renders it: "They shall be rushing with their heads raised upward."

**لَا يَرْتَدُّ إِلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ — "their gaze returning not towards them."** Ibn Kathir: "their eyes are staring in confusion, trying not to blink because of the horror and tremendous insights they are experiencing, and fear of what is going to strike them" — and he adds, "we seek refuge with Allah from this end." Maʿārif puts it as "Their eyes shall not return towards them."

**وَأَفْئِدَتُهُمْ هَوَاءٌ — "and their hearts empty."** Ibn Kathir: their hearts are empty due to extreme fear and fright. He then reports from Qatādah and several others a starker image — that *the places of their hearts* are empty then, because the hearts will ascend to the throats due to extreme fear. Maʿārif translates it "And their hearts shall be hollow."

So the picture is complete: legs hurrying, heads raised, eyes fixed, hearts hollow. Maʿārif draws the conclusion for the wrongdoers of ayah 42 — the postponement of sudden punishment against these unjust people is not any better for them, because ultimately they will be seized in the great punishment of the Qiyāmah and the Ākhirah (the Hereafter), which will overtake them all of a sudden.

## Ayah 44: the plea that comes too late

"And warn mankind of the Day when the torment will come unto them; then the wrongdoers will say: 'Our Lord! Respite us for a little while, we will answer Your call and follow the Messengers!'"

Ibn Kathir heads this section with a sentence worth memorising: *There will be no Respite after the Coming of the Torment.* Maʿārif captures the shape of the request: the unjust and the wrong-doing will have no choice but to call their Lord for some more time to return to the world they knew, so that they could say yes to the call of the prophets and follow them this time, and thereby have their deliverance from this punishment.

Ibn Kathir shows this to be a recurring reflex the Qur'an records elsewhere, not a one-off: "Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: 'My Lord! Send me back'" (23:99); "O you who believe! Let not your properties divert you" (63:9–10); "And if you only could see when the criminals shall hang their heads" (32:12); "If you could but see when they will be held over the Fire! They will say: 'Would that we were but sent back (to the world)! Then we would not deny the Ayat of Our Lord…'" (6:27); and "Therein they will cry" (35:37).

**Answered by their own oaths.** Allah refutes the plea not with a lecture but with a quotation from their own mouths: "Had you not sworn aforetime that you would not leave?" Ibn Kathir paraphrases: *Had you not vowed before that your previous state will not change, that there will be no Resurrection or Reckoning? Therefore, taste this torment because of what you vowed before.* Mujāhid commented that "you would not leave" (مَا لَكُم مِّن زَوَالٍ) refers to leaving this worldly life for the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: "And they swear by Allah with their strongest oaths, that Allah will not raise up him who dies" (16:38).

Maʿārif fills in the content of those oaths: that their wealth and power shall never part with them, that they shall go on living in the world just like that, in comfort and luxury, forever — and that they had rejected the idea that they would live again and that there was a world hereafter. The reply is devastating precisely because it is their own confidence played back to them.

## Ayah 45: living in the ruins and learning nothing

"And you dwelt in the dwellings of men who wronged themselves, and it was clear to you how We dealt with them. And We put forth (many) parables for you."

Ibn Kathir's summary is blunt: you have witnessed or heard of the news of what happened to the earlier disbelieving nations, "but you did not draw a lesson from their end, nor did what We punished them with provide an example for you." He sets beside it (54:5): "Perfect wisdom but the warners benefit [them] not."

Maʿārif is explicit that the address here is to the Mushriks of Arabia — those who associated others with Allah in worship — the very people the Prophet ﷺ was asked to warn in ayah 44 ("And warn the people"). They are told to take their guard against what could happen to them as a result of their heedlessness: the conditions past peoples faced, and the revolutions that overtook them, could become their teacher. Yet, says Maʿārif, it is astonishing that they would still prefer not to learn a lesson — even though they live in the very homes once occupied by peoples destroyed in punishment, and walk around neighbourhoods once walked by them. The truth is that they know by direct observation, and by continuing reports, how terrible was the punishment Allah Taʿālā inflicted on those peoples because of their acts of disobedience. The advice and the examples were given to bring them to see the truth and take the straight path — and it was certainly strange that they would still not listen and learn to act right.

## Ayah 46: their plot, and the mountains

Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah reads: "Indeed, they planned their plot, and their plot was with Allah, though their plot was not such as to remove the mountains from their places."

Maʿārif's rendering of the same ayah reads: "And they worked out their plot and whatever they plot is before Allah, even though their plot is such as would move the mountains."

Look at the two closing clauses. That difference is not carelessness; it is a real difference among the scholars over the last part of the verse, and both commentators lay it out.

**"Their plot was with Allah" (وَعِندَ ٱللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ).** On this much there is no dispute. Maʿārif explains that those people tried to demolish the true faith and put into action their deadliest plans to bring harm to the Muslims who had embraced the call of truth. But all plans made by them, open or concealed, lie exposed before Allah Taʿālā, who is fully aware of them and comprehensively capable of foiling them. What Maʿārif said at ayah 42 about their deeds — that everything they do is within the sight of Allah — it now says about their plans.

Whose plotting? Maʿārif allows two possibilities: the plots and plans made by peoples destroyed in the past — for example Nimrūd, Pharaoh, the people of ʿĀd and Thamūd, and others — or the many deep-seated and far-reaching conspiracies the Mushriks of Arabia hatched against the Prophet ﷺ, all of which were foiled by Allah Taʿālā.

**The mountains.** The difference turns on the small word إِن (*in*) in the closing clause. Maʿārif reports that a good many commentators have taken it as a particle of negation — a word that turns the clause into a denial — so that the verse means: though they made many plots, it was not possible for their plots to make mountains move away from their place. Ibn Kathir, for his part, preserves reports on more than one side:

- **Their plot could never move mountains.** Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the ayah indicates that their plot was not such as to remove the mountains from their places; similar was said by Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī. Ibn Jarīr reasoned that "associating others with Allah and disbelieving in Him, which they brought upon themselves, did not bother the mountains nor other creatures. Rather, the harm of their actions came to haunt them." Ibn Kathir adds his own comparison: "And walk not on the earth with conceit and arrogance. Verily, you can neither rend nor penetrate the earth, nor can you attain a stature like the mountains in height" (17:37).
- **Their plot was such as to move mountains.** Ibn Jurayj narrated that Mujāhid recited this ayah in a way that means, "though their plot was such as to remove the mountains from their places." Maʿārif's own gloss runs along these lines: their plots were so precise and lethal that they would have made mountains back out from their place — but finally, nothing worked before the perfect power of Allah Taʿālā.
- **The clause refers to their shirk.** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the clause refers to their *shirk* — their ascribing of partners to Allah — citing another ayah: "Whereby the heavens are almost torn" (19:90). Ad-Daḥḥāk and Qatādah said similarly.
