Maʿārif records one further understanding among those who read *in* as a negation: that "the mountain" here means the high determination of the Prophet ﷺ, which remained totally unaffected by any of the moves made by the disbelievers.

**The man in the box.** Ibn Kathir relates that Shuʿbah narrated that Abū Isḥāq said that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bin Dabil said that ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib commented on this clause with the case of "he who disputed with Ibrāhīm about his Lord": he took two eaglets and raised them until they became adult eagles, then tied each eagle's leg to a wooden box with ropes and left them to go hungry. He and another man sat inside the wooden box and raised a staff with a piece of meat on its tip, so the two eagles started flying. The king asked his companion to tell him what he was seeing, and the man described the scenes to him, until he said that he saw the earth as a fly. So the king brought the staff closer to the eagles and they started landing slowly. Mujāhid also mentioned that this story was about Nebuchadnezzar, and that when the king's sight was far away from the earth and its people, he was called, "O tyrant one! Where are you headed to?" He became afraid and brought the staff closer to the eagles, which flew faster with such haste that the mountains almost shook from the noise they made, and the mountains were almost moved from their places.

Whichever reading one follows, the scene lands where the whole passage lands: a man may build a machine to climb above the earth until it looks like a fly, and his plan is still lying open before Allah, who is fully aware of it and completely able to foil it.

## Living it

**If you are the one being wronged,** ayah 42 is addressed to you first — Maʿārif says the verse is, initially, to comfort the Prophet ﷺ and the oppressed of the world. Nothing has been overlooked; Ibn Kathir says full account is being kept and kept on record.

**If you are being given time,** hear the second half. Maʿārif warns the wrongdoer not to become carefree because Allah Taʿālā has given him respite, nor to be deluded into thinking that flourishing means Allah is unaware. And Ibn Kathir's heading over ayah 44 is the whole warning in one line: there will be no respite after the coming of the torment. The people of that ayah beg for a little more time in which to answer the call and follow the Messengers — the one thing they had been given already.

**And do not let history be scenery.** Ayah 45 rebukes people who lived in the very homes of peoples destroyed before them and still would not learn. Maʿārif says the examples were placed before them to bring them to see the truth and take the straight path. A sign only works if it changes what you do.

passages.title: Allah's promise kept and the final reckoning
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These six ayat close Sūrah Ibrāhīm by settling a question the whole surah has been circling: when the tyrants hold the power and the messengers are threatened, does Allah's promise really hold? Ayah 47 forbids even entertaining the doubt. Ayat 48–51 then show *where* and *when* that promise lands — on a Day when the ground beneath our feet has been exchanged for another ground, when everyone stands exposed before Allah, and when each soul is paid precisely what it earned. Ayah 52 tells us why any of this was described to us in the first place.

## Ayah 47: "Do not think Allah fails His promise"

فَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ مُخْلِفَ وَعْدِهِ رُسُلَهُ — *So do not think that Allah will fail to keep His promise to His Messengers.*

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah affirming His promise: the promise **to grant them victory in this life and on the Day when the Witnesses shall come forth**. Not one or the other — both. The vindication that history sometimes delays is never cancelled; it is only scheduled.

The address is striking. The warning lands on the Prophet ﷺ himself — *do not you think*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the purpose: it was **to let this be heard by the Muslim community** that the Prophet ﷺ — "or everyone thus addressed," as Maʿārif puts it — was given a note of caution. The person least likely to doubt the promise is the one told not to doubt it, so that everyone standing behind him hears how unthinkable the doubt is.

**"Mighty, Lord of Retribution."** The ayah seals itself with إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انتِقَامٍ. Ibn Kathir draws two things from it: that Allah is All-Able, so that **nothing He wills escapes His power and none can resist Him**; and that He is Able **to exact retribution from those who disbelieve in Him and deny Him** — quoting *Woe that Day to the deniers!* (77:15). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point in one line: He **would definitely retaliate against the enemies of His messengers and fulfil the promises made to them**. Mercy toward the messengers and reckoning against their enemies are not two policies. They are one promise seen from two sides.

## Ayah 48: the day the earth is no longer the earth

يَوْمَ تُبَدَّلُ الْأَرْضُ غَيْرَ الْأَرْضِ وَالسَّمَاوَاتُ — *the Day the earth will be changed into another earth, and the heavens too.*

Ibn Kathir ties this directly back to ayah 47: **His promise shall come to pass** on the Day when the earth is changed into **an earth other than this earth that we know and recognise**. The verse does not merely describe cosmic upheaval; it names the venue where the promise is finally honoured.

**Changed how?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the scholarly discussion honestly rather than flattening it. The words can mean that the earth's and sky's **distinctive characteristics and appearances will be changed** — the whole surface levelled into a plain with no house, tree, mountain or mound blocking the view, and no cave or abyss left. That, Maʿārif says, is the state the Qur'an describes elsewhere as لَّا تَرَىٰ فِيهَا عِوَجًا وَلَا أَمْتًا, *you will not see in it any crookedness, or curvature* (20:107). Maʿārif offers a homely image for what that means: the roads and pathways we see today wind their way past buildings and mountains, negotiating twists and turns over high and low ground; all of that becomes **flat, unobstructed ground**.

Or the words can mean that **another set of the earth and the sky would be made in the place of the present ones**. Maʿārif notes that of the narrations reported on the subject, some seem to indicate only a change in features, while others suggest a change of the thing itself.

**What the reports say.** Al-Baihaqi reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, on chains Maʿārif describes as authentic, that the Prophet ﷺ said about this verse that the ground of al-Maḥshar — the plain of Resurrection, the open ground on which humanity is assembled — **will be brand new, radiant white like silver**, a surface on which no sin was ever committed by anyone and on which no blood of anyone unjustly killed was ever shed. Maʿārif notes (citing Tafsīr Maẓharī) that the same subject appears in a hadith reported in the Musnad of Ahmad and in Tafsīr Ibn Jarīr, narrated by Anas.

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs — the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim — carry a report from Sahl ibn Saʿd. Ibn Kathir renders the Prophet's ﷺ words: **"On the Day of Resurrection, the people will be gathered on a white (barren), flat earth just like the wheat bread, it has no recognizable features for anyone."** Maʿārif renders the same narration a little differently — an earth surface **"clean and white like refined pita bread with no trace of anything else (such as house, garden, tree, mountain, mound etc.)"** — and adds that al-Baihaqi reported the same subject from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās. Two translators, one image: bare, bright, and blank.

Al-Ḥākim, on a chain Maʿārif calls strong, reports from Jābir that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Qiyāmah this earth **will be stretched like leather** so that its wrinkles and crinkles are smoothed out — caves and mountains all levelled into a flat surface — and the whole progeny of Ādam will be gathered on those plains, in such multitude that one person will have only as much land in his or her share as he or she can stand on. Then, he said, **"I shall be the first to be called on the plains of Resurrection"**; there he will fall down in prostration before his Lord, and when he is given permission to intercede, he will **intercede for the whole creation so that they go through the reckoning of their deeds swiftly**. It is worth pausing on that: in a scene built entirely of terror, the first act recorded is a prostration made on our behalf.

**Reconciling the reports.** Maʿārif itself does the work. Jābir's report, it says, seems to indicate that the change is restricted to the earth's physical features while the earth itself remains as it is; the other narrations tell us that the earth of al-Maḥshar will be an earth other than the present one — and as for the change mentioned in *this* verse, it means the change of the earth itself. Then Maʿārif quotes Maulana Ashraf Thanavi in *Bayān al-Qurʼān*: there is **no contradiction**. It is possible that the features of the present earth are changed at the time the first Horn is blown, and that people are then transferred to some other earth for the purpose of the reckoning of deeds. A saying of ʿIkrimah, found in the Musnad of ʿAbd ibn al-Ḥumayd and reported in Tafsīr Maẓharī, supports this: **"This earth will contract and it will have another earth by its side on which people will stand for reckoning."**

Maʿārif adds one more report and then a wise restraint: Ibn Jarīr reports from several Companions and Successors that the present earth and all its rivers will turn into fire at that time — in other words, all this territory which now holds the population of the world becomes the territory of Hell. And then: **the reality of things is known to Allah alone; a servant of His can do nothing but live by his commitment to Him and not go about seeking the cause of His workings.** That is the right posture for everything in this passage that outruns our imagining.

## The rabbi's questions — a scene from the Prophet's ﷺ life

The most vivid thing the sources attach to ayah 48 is a conversation. Imam Muslim records in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, from Thawbān the servant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he was standing next to the Prophet ﷺ when a Jewish rabbi came to him and said, "Peace be to you, O Muhammad." Thawbān pushed him with such force that it almost caused him to fall down. Asked why, he said, "Why did you not say, *O Messenger of Allah*?" The rabbi answered, "We call him by the name which his family gave him." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"Muhammad is indeed the name which my family gave me."**

The rabbi said, "I came to ask you about something." The Prophet ﷺ replied, **"Would it benefit you if I replied to your question?"** He said, "I will hear it with my ear." The Prophet ﷺ, poking the ground with a staff he had, said: **"Ask."**

The rabbi asked exactly the question this ayah raises: *where will the people be when the earth is changed to another earth and so are the heavens?* The Prophet ﷺ answered, **"In the darkness before the Bridge (Jasr)."** He asked who would be the first to pass it: **"The poor emigrants (Muhājirīn)."** What their welcome-gift would be when they enter Paradise: **"The caul of fish liver."** What they would have after that: **"A bull of Paradise which grazed through its pathways will be slaughtered for them."** From what they would drink: **"From a fountain whose name is Salsabīl."**

At that point the rabbi said, **"You have said the truth,"** and moved to his real errand: "I have come to ask you about something about which none of the inhabitants of the earth knows, with the exception of a Prophet or one or two other men." Again the Prophet ﷺ asked whether the answer would benefit him, and again he said he would listen. His question was about the child. The Prophet ﷺ answered him about the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman, and how the child becomes male or female **by Allah's permission**. The rabbi said, **"You have told the truth and are indeed a Prophet,"** and left. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said: **"He asked me such things that I had no knowledge of it until Allah gave it to me."**

That last sentence is the heart of the scene. The knowledge of the Unseen in this surah's closing is not the Prophet's ﷺ own possession — it is given to him by Allah. And Maʿārif draws a further point from the same narration, which it also traces to Thawbān in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim: since the people are in a dark area near the Bridge of Ṣirāṭ, **we also learn that people will be transferred from the present earth over to the other through the Bridge of Ṣirāṭ**. This matches what ʿĀ'ishah reported. Imam Ahmad recorded that she said she was the first among all people to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about this ayah: "Where will the people be then?" He said, **"On the Ṣirāṭ."** (Muslim, but not al-Bukhārī, collected this hadith; at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah also recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī said *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*.)

**"And they will appear before Allah."** وَبَرَزُوا لِلَّهِ — Ibn Kathir explains this as describing the creatures being resurrected before Allah **from their graves**. And they stand before **الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ**, *the One, the Irresistible* — Ibn Kathir: the One **who has full power and control over all things and to Whom the necks and minds are subservient**. The name is chosen with care. Those who, in ayah 47, disbelieved and denied now stand in the open before the One whose power nothing escapes, on ground that — in the words of Sahl ibn Saʿd's hadith — has no recognisable features for anyone.

## Ayat 49–50: chained in the company you chose

وَتَرَى الْمُجْرِمِينَ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُّقَرَّنِينَ فِي الْأَصْفَادِ — *and you will see the criminals that Day bound together in fetters.*

Ibn Kathir addresses the sight to the Prophet ﷺ: you will witness **the criminals who committed the crimes of *kufr*** — disbelief — **and mischief**. The key word is **muqarranīn** — not merely "chained," but **bound together, each with his or her like**. Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's own commentary on it: *Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions* (37:22); *and when the souls are joined with their bodies* (81:7); *and when they shall be thrown into a narrow place thereof, chained together, they will exclaim therein for destruction* (25:13); and the devils *bound in fetters* (38:37–38). Maʿārif says the same in plain words: each group huddled separately, and then shackled together. Sin builds companionship in this life; on that Day the companionship is welded into iron.

**Garments of tar.** سَرَابِيلُهُم مِّن قَطِرَانٍ — their garments are of *qaṭirān*. Ibn Kathir notes it is the pitch **used to coat camels**; Qatādah commented that it is **one of the fastest objects to catch fire**; Ibn ʿAbbās used to say the *qaṭirān* meant in the ayah is **dissolved lead**. Maʿārif describes it as a highly inflammable tar-like oil that would catch fire instantly. Either way the horror is the same: clothing, the thing a person wears for cover and dignity, becomes fuel worn against the skin. And وَتَغْشَىٰ وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ — *fire will cover their faces*, which Ibn Kathir pairs with *The Fire will burn their faces, and therein they will grin, with displaced lips* (23:104). The face, which people spend a lifetime shielding from shame, is exactly what nothing else covers.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded — and Muslim also collected — from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ warned about four habits carried over from *Jāhiliyyah*, the age of ignorance before Islam, that would persist in his *Ummah*, the community of his followers:

> **"Four characteristics from the time of Jahiliyyah will remain in my Ummah, since they will not abandon them: boasting about their family lineage, discrediting family ties, seeking rain through the stars, and wailing for their dead. Verily, if she who wails dies before she repents from her behavior, she will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection while wearing a dress of Qatiran and a cloak of mange."**

It is a sobering link. The garment of tar is not reserved for distant tyrants; the hadith attaches it to a habit that can live quietly inside a believing community.

## Ayah 51: paid exactly what you earned

لِيَجْزِيَ اللَّهُ كُلَّ نَفْسٍ مَّا كَسَبَتْ — *so that Allah may requite each person according to what he has earned.* Ibn Kathir: this is on the Day of Resurrection, as in *That He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done* (53:31). The little word "so that" is the purpose of the whole scene: everything from the changed earth to the chains exists so that justice can be exact.

إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ — *Truly, Allah is swift at reckoning.* Ibn Kathir: when He wills to reckon a servant of His, **He knows everything and nothing ever escapes His observation**; His power over all of His creation is the same as His power over one creature — *The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as a single person* (31:28). And this, Ibn Kathir says, is why Mujāhid glossed "swift at reckoning" as **"keeping count."** Read that way, the reckoning is not Allah discovering the record; it is the record, already complete, being shown to us.

## Ayah 52: why we were told

هَٰذَا بَلَاغٌ لِّلنَّاسِ — *This is a Message for mankind.* Ibn Kathir reads *balāgh* as a message that reaches and is conveyed, quoting *(So) that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach* (6:19): this Qur'an is for all mankind and the jinn. And he points back to the opening of this very surah — *Alif-Lām-Rā. (This is) a Book which We have revealed unto you in order that you might lead mankind out of darkness into light* (14:1). The surah closes where it began. Ibn Kathir's own commentary on Sūrah Ibrāhīm ends here, with praise of Allah.

The ayah names three purposes: **that they may be warned thereby** — Ibn Kathir: or to receive and draw lessons from it; **that they may know that He is but one Deity (ilāh wāḥid)** — using its proofs and evidences that testify that there is no true deity except Allah; and **that men of understanding may take heed** — *ulū al-albāb* in the Arabic, which Ibn Kathir glosses as those who have good minds.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the whole passage into this final purpose. The description of the conditions people will face on the Day of Qiyāmah was given **to warn them**, so that they would realise that there is no Being worthy of worship and obedience except the One Being, Allah, and so that whoever has some sense left in him or her would **desist from shirk while there was still the time to do so** — *shirk* being the association of partners with Allah.

## Living it

Read as one unit, the passage moves from *do not doubt the promise* (47), to *here is the Day it is kept* (48), to *here is what unrepented crime looks like there* (49–50), to *here is the exactness of it* (51), to *and this was told you while you can still act on it* (52). The proper response is not fascination with the details — Maʿārif itself warns against going about seeking the cause of Allah's workings when the reality of things is known to Him alone. It is the response ayah 52 asks for: take the warning seriously, hold to Allah's oneness alone, and be among those with good minds — the ones who actually let what they know reach their conduct. And take from ayah 47 the very thing it was revealed to give: settled confidence that when the promise seems slow, it is not broken. It is being kept on a Day whose ground has not yet been laid.
